A 2012 randomized trial in advanced pancreatic cancer patients (CARPAN, n=72) showed L-carnitine reduced cancer-related weight loss. The pooled standardized effect size across all studies was moderate (SMD −1.11 [−1.9 to −0.33]), favoring L-carnitine.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one primary randomized trial in the human dataset; the rest are meta-analyses and systematic reviews. Sample sizes across studies are modest to moderate (28–2292), and the evidence base is too thin for the top tier, placing it at Moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eleven human studies and ten animal studies examined glycemic control. A 2021 meta-analysis quantified L-carnitine's effect on blood sugar control in type 2 diabetes patients. A 2024 systematic review (n=2041) found improvements in glycemic indices alongside weight loss. A 2020 RCT (n=52) measured changes in fasting glucose and related markers. A 2009 RCT (n=41) in diabetic patients showed reduced oxidized LDL cholesterol, a marker of metabolic stress. A 2018 pilot study examined effects on aging muscle in older women. Across verified studies with sample sizes, approximately 2634 participants were studied, though many abstracts omitted counts, so the true total is larger.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Seven primary human trials and two pooled analyses provide evidence, but this falls below the threshold for top-tier confidence. The effect is seen in type 2 diabetes and metabolic conditions, but studies are small and heterogeneous.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine human studies and ten animal studies examined lipid profiles. A 2019 meta-analysis of randomized trials found that L-carnitine supplementation reduced serum cholesterol and triglycerides (pooled mean difference −9.47 [−13.23 to −5.7] mg/dL). A 2016 RCT (n=24) in patients with coronary artery disease showed improvements in lipid panels. A 2009 RCT (n=41) in diabetic patients reported reduced oxidized LDL cholesterol. A 2024 RCT (n=30) in pediatric ketogenic diet patients measured lipid changes. Across eight studies reporting sample size, approximately 574 participants were analyzed, though the true total is likely larger.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: One meta-analysis exists, but it has not been independently replicated or verified in separate trials. The consistency is supported by small- to moderate-sized RCTs in specific populations (diabetes, coronary disease), but the evidence base remains limited for broad application.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies (mostly systematic reviews) and two animal studies examined acute and chronic L-carnitine effects on exercise performance. A 2021 systematic review synthesized effects of acute and chronic oral L-carnitine on exercise performance across different exercise types. A 2020 systematic review (n=11 verified participants across measured arms) found mixed results. A 2025 RCT on acute L-carnitine supplementation in CrossFit athletes showed no improvement in performance. Animal studies from 2012 and 2026 examined mitochondrial effects and nutrient handling in cells.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only three human studies retrieved, with verified sample size of just 11 across measured trials. This is far below the threshold for meaningful statistical confidence. Results are inconsistent (one negative acute trial, mixed findings in reviews), and no large RCT in athletes has been located in the provided records.

l-carnitine::clarity-engine::rich7::8d2c.evidence_base: The evidence is dominated by small to moderate human RCTs (most 20–72 participants) and meta-analyses pooling them, published primarily in the last 10 years (2018–2025). Animal studies provide cellular and mechanistic support but do not directly translate to humans. The human trials focus on type 2 diabetes, obesity, and cancer-related weight loss; exercise performance data are sparse and inconsistent. This is a tested area but with modest, replicated findings rather than robust proof.
l-carnitine::clarity-engine::rich7::8d2c.open_questions: The retrieved records show L-carnitine studied mainly in adults with metabolic disease or cancer; trials in healthy, athletic, or young populations are rare or absent. Most studies last weeks to a few months — long-term (>6 months) effects are underrepresented. Whether L-carnitine helps prevent age-related muscle loss, whether it works in people with normal carnitine levels, and how it performs compared to lifestyle changes (diet, exercise) alone are not clearly addressed in the records provided. Exercise performance data are too thin to draw conclusions; this remains an open question.

lion's mane::clarity-engine::rich7::1a9b.what_it_is_line: A culinary mushroom extract claimed to support brain health and mood
lion's mane::clarity-engine::rich7::1a9b.what_it_is: Lion's Mane (Hericium erinaceus) is an edible mushroom that grows on hardwood trees, native to Asia and North America. It contains bioactive compounds — mostly polysaccharides and proteins — that are extracted and concentrated into supplements. People typically take it as a powder, capsule, or liquid extract by mouth.
lion's mane::clarity-engine::rich7::1a9b.how_it_works_line: Appears to stimulate nerve growth factor, a protein that helps brain cells survive and form new connections
lion's mane::clarity-engine::rich7::1a9b.how_it_works: Lion's Mane contains compounds that may increase nerve growth factor (NGF) — a signaling molecule your brain cells rely on to grow, survive, and wire themselves together. More NGF is thought to help protect existing neurons and encourage the formation of new connections between brain cells, which underlies learning and memory. The mushroom also contains polysaccharides that may reduce inflammatory signals (molecules that trigger immune activation and tissue damage) in the brain and body. Animal studies suggest these mechanisms could support cognitive resilience and mood, but it remains unclear whether the doses and delivery methods used in human supplements achieve these effects in the brain.
lion's mane::clarity-engine::rich7::1a9b.safety_line: Mild to no adverse effects reported in short-term trials; long-term safety and drug interactions unknown
lion's mane::clarity-engine::rich7::1a9b.safety_detail: The human trials retrieved reported minimal side effects — mostly mild gastrointestinal symptoms in a small number of participants — over study periods of weeks to months. However, these studies did not comprehensively measure safety in long-term use, and the exact sample sizes and adverse event rates could not be verified from the abstracts alone.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety (beyond a few months) has not been adequately tested in the provided records
Drug interactions with immunosuppressants or anticoagulants (blood thinners) are untested; caution is warranted if you take these
Safety in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and children is not addressed in the retrieved trials — use is therefore unverified in these populations
lion's mane::clarity-engine::rich7::1a9b.chem_meaning: Lion's Mane extracts are water-soluble, meaning they dissolve in aqueous environments like the digestive system and bloodstream. This favors absorption but also means the active compounds depend on efficient uptake across the gut wall — a process that may vary between individuals and formulations.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2023 randomized controlled trial and a 2019 systematic review of dietary mushroom supplementation both found associations between Lion's Mane supplementation and cognitive improvements. The 2023 trial measured acute and chronic effects on cognitive function, stress, and mood; the 2019 review synthesized in-vivo studies on mushroom supplementation for cognitive impairment. Actual sample sizes and effect magnitudes could not be verified from the abstracts provided.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two human studies show consistent direction of effect, but sample-size precision is unconfirmed and no independent replication of the 2019 review conclusion exists, so certainty is held at Moderate rather than Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2023 randomized controlled trial examined the effects of Lion's Mane supplementation on mood alongside cognitive function and stress measures. The trial was designed to assess both acute and chronic effects, but sample size details could not be confirmed from the abstract.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study addresses this outcome, so consistency across independent evidence cannot be assessed. Precision is also unconfirmed, placing this at Emerging — promising but requiring replication.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: The same 2023 randomized controlled trial that measured mood also measured stress and anxiety outcomes alongside cognition. Exact sample sizes and stress/anxiety effect sizes could not be verified from the abstract.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study addresses this outcome with no independent replication, and precision is unconfirmed. This places stress/anxiety at Emerging — a promising early signal that needs independent testing.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2015 animal study demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects of Lion's Mane in an experimental model. The study measured inflammatory markers in response to the mushroom extract, but results were obtained in animals, not humans.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is animal-only and does not reliably predict human outcomes. Whether Lion's Mane reduces inflammation in people remains untested.

lion's mane::clarity-engine::rich7::1a9b.evidence_base: The evidence base consists of two human studies (both from 2023 or earlier) — one randomized controlled trial and one systematic review — plus one animal study on inflammation. Human evidence is limited and covers relatively short time frames; no long-term human trials were retrieved. The body of evidence is recent but small, so confidence in any effect is modest and contingent on replication.
lion's mane::clarity-engine::rich7::1a9b.open_questions: The retrieved records do not adequately specify sample sizes, effect sizes, or trial durations, limiting precision assessment. Cognition appears in two human records (one review, one trial), but mood and stress rest on a single 2023 trial with unverified sample details — replication in independent populations is essential. Inflammation evidence is animal-only; whether the anti-inflammatory mechanism translates to humans has not been tested in the provided records. Notably absent are studies in aging populations, clinical depression or anxiety diagnoses, or neurological disease — populations most likely to benefit if the mechanism is real.

manganese::clarity-engine::rich7::5935c7.what_it_is_line: A metallic element essential for bone, enzyme, and immune function in the body.
manganese::clarity-engine::rich7::5935c7.what_it_is: Manganese is a naturally occurring metal found in soil, water, and many foods — nuts, seeds, grains, leafy greens, and tea are rich sources. Your body contains only a small amount, but it is an essential micronutrient, meaning you need it to survive and function. People typically get manganese from food; supplements are available as powders, tablets, or injections, often in forms like manganese gluconate or manganese oxide.
manganese::clarity-engine::rich7::5935c7.how_it_works_line: Activates enzymes that protect cells from damage and support bone and immune development.
manganese::clarity-engine::rich7::5935c7.how_it_works: Manganese works primarily as a cofactor — a helper molecule that allows certain enzymes to function. One of the most important is superoxide dismutase (SOD), an enzyme that neutralizes free radicals (unstable molecules that damage cells). It also plays a role in bone formation by activating enzymes needed to build the mineral matrix that gives bone its strength, and in immune cell development by supporting the maturation and activation of white blood cells. The full scope of how manganese supports immune and metabolic function in humans is not completely mapped, but animal studies suggest these pathways are real and consequential.
manganese::clarity-engine::rich7::5935c7.safety_line: Short-term supplementation appears tolerated in animal trials; human safety data is very limited.
manganese::clarity-engine::rich7::5935c7.safety_detail: The retrieved studies on manganese supplementation in animals reported no serious adverse events in the trials described, but these were typically short-term and conducted in poultry and livestock, not humans. The one human study (a cross-sectional/longitudinal dietary survey in Iranian adults) did not focus on supplementation safety. Manganese toxicity is a known risk at high doses, especially in occupational or neurological contexts, but the safety ceiling for oral supplementation in healthy adults has not been clearly established in the literature provided.
safety_bullets: Human supplementation safety is untested — all retrieved efficacy data come from animals or a single observational dietary study; no randomized controlled trials of manganese supplementation in humans were found.
Chronic high-dose manganese exposure is associated with neurological toxicity (manganism); the safe upper intake level is not defined in the records provided, and individual tolerance is unknown.
Use in kidney disease, liver disease, or during pregnancy and lactation is not addressed in any retrieved trial — effect and safety in these populations are completely untested.
Potential for drug interactions (e.g., with tetracycline antibiotics and some bisphosphonates) is not discussed in the provided studies.
manganese::clarity-engine::rich7::5935c7.chem_meaning: Manganese (Mn) is a transition metal with atomic weight ~55, meaning it can exist in multiple oxidation states — it commonly appears as Mn2+ or Mn3+ in biological systems. This chemical flexibility is what allows it to activate enzymes and participate in electron transfer reactions that neutralize free radicals. In supplements, it is usually bound to organic acids (like gluconate) or presented as an oxide to improve absorption in the gut.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human observational study (2025, n=4,384 Iranian adults) found a cross-sectional and longitudinal association between dietary manganese intake and bone health markers. Three animal studies (2024–2025) in rodents or poultry showed that manganese supplementation enhanced bone growth, skeletal development, and the osteogenic (bone-forming) effects of other compounds like silicon-hydroxyapatite. None of these were randomized controlled trials in humans, so causation cannot be inferred.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study exists, making consistency across independent evidence impossible. The remainder are animal models, which do not reliably predict human outcomes. The human evidence is observational (correlation, not proof of cause), and the sample sizes of animal studies are often not reported.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five animal studies (2019–2026, primarily in poultry; one n=120, one n=560) showed that manganese supplementation enhanced markers of immune competence — including antibody responses to vaccination, white blood cell counts, and resistance to bacterial infection in models of immune challenge. These were mostly randomized controlled trials in animals, suggesting a real biological effect, but no human trials were retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence is animal-only and does not reliably translate to humans. There is no human data to confirm whether these immune improvements occur in people.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two animal studies (2023–2024, in sheep and poultry) examined the effect of organic manganese supplementation on blood glucose and related biochemical markers. Both were conducted in livestock and reported improvements in metabolic markers, but neither included human participants.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Both studies are animal-only with no human evidence. The findings are suggestive but cannot be assumed to apply to blood sugar control in people.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven animal studies (2020–2026, primarily in poultry; sample sizes 30–896 where reported) demonstrated that manganese supplementation increased antioxidant enzyme activity (especially superoxide dismutase and catalase) and reduced markers of oxidative damage (lipid peroxides, etc.) in blood and tissue. These were mostly randomized designs in production animals, providing consistent mechanistic evidence, but zero human trials were identified.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence is animal-only. While the consistency across multiple animal studies is encouraging, animal models of oxidative stress do not reliably predict clinical antioxidant effects in humans.

manganese::clarity-engine::rich7::5935c7.evidence_base: Manganese has very limited human evidence — only one observational dietary study addressing bone health was retrieved, yielding an Emerging grade. The bulk of the literature consists of randomized or controlled animal studies (mostly poultry and rodent models) published 2019–2026. These provide mechanistic plausibility for immune, metabolic, and antioxidant roles, but animal evidence alone does not establish efficacy or safety in people. The recency of publication (mostly 2023 onward) suggests active research interest, but translation to human clinical outcomes remains untested.
manganese::clarity-engine::rich7::5935c7.open_questions: The sample includes only ~40 abstracts per outcome, a fraction of the total literature. Within these records, no randomized controlled trials of manganese supplementation in healthy humans were found — the human evidence rests on a single cross-sectional/longitudinal dietary survey. It is unknown whether the promising immune and antioxidant effects seen in poultry and rodents occur in people, at what dose, or in which populations (e.g., deficient vs. replete individuals, older adults, athletes). Long-term safety and optimal intake levels in humans have not been characterized in the provided studies.

metformin::clarity-engine::rich7::08506b.what_it_is_line: Common diabetes drug; oral biguanide that lowers blood sugar by reducing liver glucose output.
metformin::clarity-engine::rich7::08506b.what_it_is: Metformin is a small molecule (C₄H₁₁N₅) — one of the oldest and most widely prescribed diabetes medications, first synthesized decades ago and now used by millions worldwide. It belongs to a class called biguanides. People take it as an oral tablet or powder, typically once or twice daily. Because it is water-loving (XLogP −1.3), it dissolves easily in the body's fluids and does not accumulate in fatty tissue.
metformin::clarity-engine::rich7::08506b.how_it_works_line: Reduces glucose production in the liver; improves how muscle and fat cells take up sugar from blood.
metformin::clarity-engine::rich7::08506b.how_it_works: Metformin works mainly by turning down the liver's production of glucose (blood sugar) — it does this by activating an enzyme pathway called AMP-activated protein kinase, or AMPK, which acts like a metabolic brake. It also makes muscle and fat cells more responsive to insulin (the hormone that lets cells absorb sugar), so they pull more glucose from the bloodstream. In the gut, metformin alters the balance of bacteria, which may influence metabolism and weight. The exact molecular lock-and-key details are still being refined, but decades of clinical use show the overall effect is reliable: it lowers fasting blood sugar and improves how the body handles glucose throughout the day.
metformin::clarity-engine::rich7::08506b.safety_line: Well-tolerated in most people; GI side effects common; rare serious risk in severe kidney disease.
metformin::clarity-engine::rich7::08506b.safety_detail: Metformin has been used clinically for over 60 years, and retrieved trials show it is generally well-tolerated, with the most frequent side effect being gastrointestinal upset (bloating, diarrhea, nausea), which often improves with continued use or dose adjustment. A 2022 meta-analysis in the records found GI adverse events reported across many type 2 diabetes trials. Serious concerns are rare in people with normal kidney function, but metformin can accumulate dangerously if kidneys are severely impaired, and it is typically avoided or dose-reduced in such cases.
safety_bullets: Kidney function: metformin is contraindicated or requires dose adjustment in severe renal impairment; most trials enroll people with normal to mild kidney disease, so safety in advanced kidney disease is untested in the retrieved records.

Pregnancy: high-dose or prolonged use is not routinely studied in pregnant populations; a 2026 meta-analysis in the records examined metformin in metabolic-risk pregnancies, but safety profile for fetal development remains incompletely characterized.
Vitamin B12 absorption: long-term use may reduce B12 levels in some people; this was not a primary focus in retrieved trials, so the true incidence and clinical significance are unclear.

Drug interactions: metformin has few major interactions, but co-administration with contrast dye (used in some imaging) requires temporary discontinuation; specific interactions with other supplements are not extensively addressed in the retrieved records.
metformin::clarity-engine::rich7::08506b.chem_meaning: Metformin is a small, water-loving molecule that dissolves readily in blood and body fluids. Its negative lipophilicity (XLogP −1.3) means it does not store in fat and instead circulates freely, which is why it needs to be dosed regularly and why it concentrates in the kidney. This water-soluble nature also makes it safe to use orally without concern for fat-tissue accumulation, and it is readily filtered and cleared by the kidneys.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Metformin reliably lowers fasting blood glucose across diverse populations. A pooled analysis of human studies showed a mean reduction of ~0.06 mmol/L (95% CI −0.1 to −0.01), consistent across approximately 6,369 verified participants in 16 of 42 studies retrieved. Six independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews on blood sugar control converge on this finding, indicating robust replication. Recent trials (2023–2026) include pregnant women at metabolic risk (n=2,695), people with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS, n=1,691), and those undergoing exercise interventions (n=325), all confirming glucose-lowering efficacy.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong evidence rests on large, pooled human populations, multiple independent meta-analyses reaching the same conclusion, and consistent effect across different patient groups (pregnancy, PCOS, diabetes). The effect size is modest but reproducible and clinically meaningful for glucose management.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Metformin is associated with modest weight loss in some populations. Four human and two animal studies were retrieved; human evidence includes a 2021 randomized controlled trial (n=121) showing metformin altered gut microbiota composition and circulating short-chain fatty acids (metabolites linked to energy harvest and satiety), a 2023 meta-analysis in PCOS patients, and a 2025 trial examining side effects during cancer chemotherapy. A 2008 trial (n=20) in women with PCOS found metformin increased circulating PYY, a hormone that suppresses appetite. Total verified participants: ~141 across 2 of 6 studies; most abstracts do not report sample sizes, so true population is larger.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is moderate: only four human primary/meta-analysis records retrieved, and a single meta-analysis conclusion with no independent replication. Weight loss appears mechanistically plausible through gut microbiota and appetite-hormone pathways, but the human efficacy signal is weaker and less replicated than blood sugar control.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Metformin alters gut function and microbiota composition. Thirteen human and ten animal studies were retrieved; pooled meta-analysis showed an odds ratio of 7.67 (95% CI 2.74–21.46) for gastrointestinal adverse events (mainly diarrhea and bloating), reported across ~5,322 verified participants in 9 of 23 studies. A 2022 meta-analysis specifically catalogued GI adverse events in type 2 diabetes patients. Beyond side effects, a 2021 RCT (n=121) documented metformin-driven shifts in gut bacterial composition and increased short-chain fatty acids, suggesting altered microbiota function rather than simple toxicity. Studies span pregnancies (n=2,695), PCOS (n=1,691), and diabetes trials, suggesting broad effects on the GI tract.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate evidence: 13 human studies and multiple meta-analyses, but the dominant signal is GI adverse events (side effect), not a therapeutic benefit. Microbiota changes are documented but interpreted cautiously; their functional significance for health outcomes beyond weight/metabolism is not fully characterized in the retrieved records. Limited human evidence (7 primary studies) below top-tier threshold.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Metformin produces modest changes in blood lipid profiles. Five human and two animal studies were retrieved. A 2026 RCT (n=180) examined oral contraceptive and metformin effects on advanced lipid phenotyping in PCOS; a 2024 RCT compared metformin–atorvastatin combination versus monotherapy in type 2 diabetes; a 2019 trial (n=27) found metformin induced changes in sphingolipid species and oxidized lipids in PCOS women. A 2014 study suggested metformin mitigates cell death in ischemic heart tissue (potential cardioprotection). Total verified participants: ~207 across 2 of 7 studies; most abstracts omit sample sizes. Animal studies examined oxidized LDL and macrophage inflammation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate evidence: only five human records and two animal studies. A single meta-analysis conclusion exists with no independent replication. Lipid changes appear modest and appear to overlap with effects on PCOS and metabolic syndrome rather than being a primary indication; the clinical significance of lipid shifts is not fully established in the retrieved records.

metformin::clarity-engine::rich7::08506b.evidence_base: Metformin's evidence base is predominantly human and clinical, reflecting its long history as a FDA-approved drug. Across all four outcomes, 27 human studies (including randomized controlled trials, clinical trials, and meta-analyses) and 15 animal studies were retrieved, with the earliest dating to 2008 and most recent to 2026. Blood sugar control is most robustly supported by six independent meta-analyses and ~6,369 pooled participants, whereas weight loss, GI effects, and lipid changes rest on fewer primary studies and single meta-analyses. The retrieved records represent a sample of ~40 abstracts per outcome and do not constitute an exhaustive literature review; the true scope of metformin research is substantially larger. High replication of the blood sugar outcome across populations and decades justifies a Strong grade; the other outcomes, supported by moderate human evidence and single meta-analyses, are held at Moderate.
metformin::clarity-engine::rich7::08506b.open_questions: Within the records provided, blood sugar control is documented across pregnant women, PCOS patients, and those with type 2 diabetes or metabolic syndrome, indicating broad applicability; weight loss and lipid changes are heavily weighted toward PCOS and metabolic-risk populations, leaving open whether benefits generalize to other groups. GI side effects are well-catalogued, but the microbiota-mediated mechanisms linking metformin to weight or metabolic benefit remain incompletely characterized—most retrieved abstracts describe the bacterial shift without proving its causal role. Notably absent from the retrieved records are large, long-term trials in healthy, normal-weight individuals or older adults aiming at lifespan or age-related disease prevention (the 'longevity' category claimed), meaning any anti-aging claim rests on inference from metabolic and cardiovascular surrogate markers, not direct evidence of life extension in humans.

nr::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73bf7fcc.what_it_is_line: A form of vitamin B3 that cells convert to NAD+, a molecule essential for energy and aging.
nr::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73bf7fcc.what_it_is: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring compound related to vitamin B3. It consists of the vitamin nicotinamide bonded to a five-carbon sugar (ribose). Your cells absorb NR and convert it into NAD+, a molecule that sits at the center of energy production and cellular repair. NR is sold as an oral supplement and is also found in small amounts in cow's milk and whey protein.
nr::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73bf7fcc.how_it_works_line: Replenishes NAD+, the fuel for cellular energy and repair machinery that declines with age.
nr::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73bf7fcc.how_it_works: NAD+ is a coenzyme — a helper molecule that cells use to transfer energy during metabolism and to power repair processes. As you age, NAD+ levels naturally drop, which may impair your cells' ability to make energy efficiently and to fix DNA damage. NR is a precursor: your cells take it up and convert it through enzymatic steps into NAD+, thereby restoring the pool of this molecule. In cell cultures and animal models, raising NAD+ levels has been shown to activate sirtuins and other 'longevity' proteins that are thought to promote cellular repair and slow aging processes. Whether boosting NAD+ in humans produces those same effects remains an open question; the field is actively testing this.
nr::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73bf7fcc.safety_line: Mostly well-tolerated in short trials; long-term and vulnerable-population safety remain untested.
nr::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73bf7fcc.safety_detail: Short-term studies (weeks to a few months) in generally healthy adults have reported few serious adverse events, with most participants completing trials without major problems. However, no adequately powered long-term safety trials have been retrieved, and NR has been excluded from most trials in elderly, pregnant, kidney-impaired, and pediatric populations, so safety in those groups is unknown.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety (beyond 12 months) not established in retrieved records.

Untested in pregnancy, kidney or liver disease, and pediatric populations — mechanism suggests potential effects on cellular metabolism that could pose risk in vulnerable groups, but no data retrieved.
Drug interaction potential not systematically studied; NAD+-dependent pathways could theoretically interact with medications affecting metabolism, but this remains speculative.
High-dose safety unknown; most trials use modest doses (250–1000 mg/day) for short periods.
nr::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73bf7fcc.chem_meaning: NR is a moderately water-loving molecule (XLogP –1.8), meaning it dissolves well in water and can be absorbed from the gut without requiring fatty food. Its relatively small size (~255 Da) and charged pyridinium ring allow it to cross some cellular membranes efficiently, which is why it can be taken orally and reach cells throughout the body.
nr::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73bf7fcc.evidence_base: No human trials with efficacy outcomes meeting grading criteria were retrieved for NR in the provided records. The compound has been studied in cell cultures and animal models (mainly mice and rodents), where increased NAD+ levels have been associated with improvements in metabolic markers, mitochondrial function, and longevity-related pathways. Human trials so far have focused on tolerability and NAD+ bioavailability (whether the body can absorb it and convert it to NAD+), not on clinical endpoints such as lifespan, age-related disease prevention, or functional aging. This reflects the early stage of human translation for NAD+-boosting compounds.
nr::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73bf7fcc.open_questions: The provided records show no human efficacy trials for longevity or age-related outcomes. The evidence base consists primarily of mechanistic studies in cells and short-term bioavailability studies in healthy adults. Notably absent from the records are long-term studies in older adults, trials in disease models (cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, metabolic), and comparisons to other NAD+ precursors. Whether NR can slow aging or prevent age-related disease in humans is not yet known and remains a central unanswered question.

phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine::rich.what_it_is_line: A lipid molecule found in cell membranes; used as a dietary supplement for brain and mood support.
phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine::rich.what_it_is: Phosphatidylserine is a fatty compound (a phospholipid) that naturally occurs in the membranes of your cells, especially brain cells. It has a complex structure: a backbone of glycerol (a simple sugar alcohol) attached to two long fatty acid chains and a phosphate group (a chemical unit containing phosphorus). People take it as a supplement in capsule form, often derived from soy or sunflower sources, in doses typically ranging from 100–300 mg per day.
phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine::rich.how_it_works_line: Supports cell membranes and may influence stress hormones and brain signaling pathways.
phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine::rich.how_it_works: Phosphatidylserine is a key structural component of cell membranes — it helps keep the outer layer of cells intact and flexible, which is especially important in brain cells. Because of its chemical structure (a large, fat-soluble molecule with a molecular weight of 792), it can easily cross into fatty tissues, including the brain. Research in animal models suggests it may dampen the stress hormone cortisol and modulate how cells respond to oxidative damage (free radicals). In cells, it appears to activate signaling pathways related to cell survival and stress resistance — though the exact mechanisms in humans remain incompletely understood and most detailed data come from laboratory and animal studies.
phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine::rich.safety_line: Mild side effects reported in trials; long-term safety and drug interactions remain untested.
phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine::rich.safety_detail: Trials lasting weeks to several months reported good tolerability, with side effects (if any) generally mild and similar to placebo. However, most studies were short-term, and adequately powered trials examining long-term use (months to years) or in special populations have not been retrieved.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions: unknown — no trials retrieved examining co-use with medications; potential interactions with anticoagulants or NSAIDs are not confirmed in humans.
Pregnancy and lactation: untested — phosphatidylserine was excluded from nearly all trials, so safety in pregnant or breastfeeding women is unknown.
Kidney or liver disease: untested — no retrieved trials examined use in people with organ impairment.
Long-term safety (>6 months): not adequately powered — most trials are short-term; chronic use safety is not established.
phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine::rich.chem_meaning: Phosphatidylserine is a large, fat-soluble molecule (XLogP 12.1, meaning strongly lipophilic — water-averse). This property allows it to dissolve in and integrate into cell membranes and fatty tissues like the brain, rather than dissolving in blood. Its size and complexity mean it is not easily absorbed from food alone, which is why supplementation is used; it must be ingested or derived from specific dietary sources to achieve meaningful levels.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and two animal studies examined phosphatidylserine's effects on memory, attention, and cognitive performance. A 1993 multicenter RCT (n=494) in elderly participants showed benefit on cognitive decline; a 2014 trial (n=19) found improvements in attention-deficit symptoms; a 2008 trial measured cognitive performance after stress; and a 2026 trial examined football-specific cognitive performance. A 2026 systematic review summarized citicoline/phosphatidylserine combinations. Animal models (2020) showed it enhanced stress resilience and lifespan through a cell-survival pathway. Effect sizes varied, and most individual trials had modest sample sizes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple human RCTs with consistent direction of benefit meet the threshold for Moderate; however, a single systematic review (not independently replicated) and imprecision in sample-size reporting across studies prevent a Strong grade. The true participant count is substantially larger than verified (>513), but exact totals are unclear from abstracts.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human RCTs and one animal study examined phosphatidylserine and stress responses. A 2008 RCT measured cortical activity and cognitive performance after induced stress; a 1990 trial assessed the neuroendocrine (hormone) response to physical stress in humans; a 2006 trial examined exercise capacity during cycling. Animal work (2020) showed phosphatidylserine modulated oxidative stress responses via a hormesis pathway. Human trials generally measured cortisol and stress-related performance, but sample sizes were not consistently reported in abstracts.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple human RCTs show benefit for stress markers and resilience, justifying Moderate. Imprecision (unconfirmed sample sizes) and small sample numbers in individual studies prevent higher certainty. No major inconsistencies were apparent, but the evidence base is limited.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human trials and one animal study addressed mood and depressive symptoms. A 1990 clinical trial studied phosphatidylserine in geriatric patients with depressive disorders; a 2006 RCT examined mood during exercise; a 2021 meta-analysis reviewed phosphatidylserine in pediatric ADHD (which often co-occurs with mood dysregulation); a 2026 trial assessed behavioral problems in children with ADHD; a 2026 systematic review covered citicoline/phosphatidylserine. An animal study (2021) showed neuroprotective liposomes containing phosphatidylserine reduced depressive-like behavior after stroke. Most human trials were small and focused on ADHD-related mood effects rather than primary depression.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Five human trials with consistent benefit signal justify Moderate; however, unconfirmed sample sizes and a focus on ADHD-adjacent outcomes rather than independent depression samples limit certainty. A single meta-analysis in ADHD populations exists, but replication across depression-specific cohorts is not evident in the records provided.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two animal studies examined phosphatidylserine and lipid metabolism. A 2026 animal trial showed improvement in metabolic liver disease and glycemic control; a 2021 study described phosphatidylserine-containing liposomes as having therapeutic potential against hypercholesterolemia and atherosclerosis. No human trials on cholesterol or lipid profiles were retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is animal-only, and animal lipid metabolism does not reliably predict human responses. These findings are promising preclinical observations but do not constitute evidence of efficacy in people; human trials would be needed to establish any clinical benefit.

phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine::rich.evidence_base: The evidence is predominantly human, with 13 human studies (mostly RCTs and a systematic review) across cognition, stress, and mood outcomes. Most trials are from 1990–2026, with several from the last 5 years. Animal studies (n=4) provide mechanistic support but cannot alone establish human efficacy. Sample sizes in human trials vary (verified range ~19–494 for cognition; unconfirmed for stress and mood), and most trials are short-term (weeks to a few months). A single systematic review in citicoline/phosphatidylserine combinations exists, but independent meta-analyses and large long-term trials are not evident in the records.
phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine::rich.open_questions: The provided records show that cognition and mood outcomes are most frequently studied in adults and elderly populations, with some pediatric ADHD data; adolescents and younger adults appear underrepresented. Whether benefits persist beyond a few months is unclear, as most trials are short-term. Cholesterol/lipid effects rest on two animal studies alone — human testing has not yet occurred. The records represent approximately 40 abstracts and do not capture the full body of literature; only visible gaps in the records provided are flagged here.

psyllium fiber::clarity-engine::rich7::c.what_it_is_line: Soluble fiber from psyllium seeds; absorbs water to bulk stool and feed gut bacteria.
psyllium fiber::clarity-engine::rich7::c.what_it_is: Psyllium is a soluble fiber — a carbohydrate that your digestive system cannot break down — extracted from the seeds of the Plantago ovata plant. When you ingest it, it absorbs water and forms a thick, gel-like substance in your intestines. People typically take it as a powder mixed with water, or in capsule form. Because your own cells cannot digest it, the fiber passes through largely intact, but your gut bacteria can ferment it, which may influence how your digestive system and metabolism function.
psyllium fiber::clarity-engine::rich7::c.how_it_works_line: Absorbs water to bulk stool; fermented by gut bacteria, altering microbiota and metabolism.
psyllium fiber::clarity-engine::rich7::c.how_it_works: Psyllium works through two main pathways. First, it absorbs water in your intestines and increases stool bulk, which promotes normal bowel movement and can help regulate both constipation and diarrhea. Second, your gut bacteria ferment the fiber, producing short-chain fatty acids (small metabolic byproducts) and shifting which bacterial species thrive in your colon. This shift in the microbial community and the metabolites they produce can influence intestinal inflammation, glucose absorption, and lipid (fat) metabolism — though exactly how this translates to changes in blood sugar or cholesterol in people remains incompletely understood.
psyllium fiber::clarity-engine::rich7::c.safety_line: Generally well-tolerated in short trials; long-term safety and effects in specific populations untested.
psyllium fiber::clarity-engine::rich7::c.safety_detail: The retrieved human trials reported mild gastrointestinal side effects (bloating, gas, minor cramping) at rates comparable to placebo, and most studies lasted weeks to a few months. However, the trials included narrow populations — mainly adults with specific conditions or pediatric patients with functional abdominal pain — and no adequately powered studies were found examining long-term use (years) or safety in populations like those with severe kidney disease, active bowel obstruction, or pregnant women.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions: Not systematically studied in the retrieved trials; psyllium may delay oral medication absorption if taken simultaneously — timing separation typically recommended but not formally tested.

Excluded or unstudied populations: Pregnant women, patients with active gastrointestinal obstruction, severe renal impairment, and very young children (<6 years) appear absent from the trial records provided.
Long-term effects unknown: All retrieved studies are short-term (weeks to <1 year); safety of daily use over years is not documented in the records.
psyllium fiber::clarity-engine::rich7::c.chem_meaning: Psyllium is a large, hydrophilic (water-loving) polysaccharide that swells dramatically when hydrated. This bulk-forming property is its defining chemical characteristic — it does not dissolve, but rather absorbs and traps water, physically altering stool consistency. It is not absorbed systemically, so it remains in the gastrointestinal tract where it exerts local effects on transit and microbial fermentation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human randomized trials (RCTs) examined psyllium's effects on gut function. These included studies in enteral tube-fed patients (2019), children with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS; 2017, n=47), functional abdominal pain (2024, n=209), constipation in older adults (1995), and microbiota engraftment after fecal transplant (2025, n=27). Most found improvements in bowel regularity, abdominal pain, or stool consistency. Three animal studies (including 2024 and 2018 work) showed psyllium altered intestinal barrier function and microbial composition. Verified sample size across three human studies totaled ~283 participants, though most abstracts omitted exact numbers, suggesting the true total is considerably larger.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple human RCTs exist and show consistent direction (improvement in digestive symptoms), but no formal pooled analysis confirms they agree on effect size. Sample sizes are modest and inconsistency across populations (pediatric, elderly, specific diagnoses) prevents certainty. Hence Moderate rather than Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies, including one meta-analysis (2015), assessed psyllium's effect on fasting or postprandial (after-meal) glucose. A 1991 RCT in non-insulin-dependent diabetic patients found reduced glucose and insulin spikes after meals. The 2015 meta-analysis reported a pooled difference of −37.0 mg/dL (95% CI: −74.0 to 0.0), indicating a modest reduction, though the confidence interval includes zero, meaning the true effect is uncertain. Studies span 1985–2015; sample sizes could not be verified from abstracts.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one meta-analysis synthesizes the evidence, and it has not been independently replicated. The pooled estimate suggests a possible benefit but is imprecise (confidence interval crosses zero). Human evidence exists but is sparse and unpooled across independent trials. Moderate reflects plausible signal with modest, unconfirmed precision.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies, including a 2015 meta-analysis, examined effects on total cholesterol or lipid profiles. A 1990 RCT (n=30) in hypercholesterolemic patients reported synergistic cholesterol-lowering when psyllium was combined with diet. A 1996 study tested psyllium with soybean or coconut oil-rich diets and noted hypocholesterolemic effects. A 2008 trial (n not stated) compared pre- and post-menopausal women. The 2015 meta-analysis included lipid data, though the cholesterol findings appear less emphasized than glucose. Verified sample size is modest (~30 participants in one trial), and most abstract details are sparse.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one independent meta-analysis and small, older RCTs; no replicated pooled estimate or recent large trials. Modest verified sample sizes and inconsistent reporting prevent high confidence. Evidence suggests a signal but certainty is low, hence Moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human RCT (2008, n=158) measured C-reactive protein (CRP, a marker of systemic inflammation) and found psyllium supplementation reduced CRP in the Trial to Reduce Inflammatory Markers (TRIM). Two animal studies (2024, 2018) showed psyllium reduced inflammatory markers in the intestine and liver and improved intestinal barrier integrity. The human study is the sole independent human evidence for this outcome; consistency across human trials cannot be assessed.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study directly examines inflammation; animal data are supportive but do not substitute for human confirmation. Single human trial prevents assessment of consistency or replicability. Moderate reflects plausible biological mechanism (via microbiota and metabolite shifts) but sparse human validation.

psyllium fiber::clarity-engine::rich7::c.evidence_base: The evidence base is predominantly human RCTs and one meta-analysis (2015), spanning 1985–2025, with sample sizes mostly modest and inconsistently reported. Verified participants across key studies range from ~27 to ~283 per outcome. Animal studies (2018, 2024) provide mechanistic support but are not primary evidence. Recency is mixed: some foundational work is from the 1990s, but recent trials (2024–2025) confirm earlier findings. This moderate evidence base suggests plausible benefits but does not yet prove efficacy convincingly.
psyllium fiber::clarity-engine::rich7::c.open_questions: The records provided show RCTs in specific populations (children with IBS, elderly with constipation, diabetic patients, hypercholesterolemic adults), but represent only a sample of the broader literature (~40 abstracts per outcome). Duration of most trials is short (weeks to months); long-term efficacy and whether benefits persist beyond 6–12 months remain unclear in the provided records. No large, multi-center trials directly comparing psyllium to active controls (vs. placebo alone) appear in the sample. Whether effects vary by baseline microbiota composition, age, sex, or metabolic status is suggested by some data (e.g., sex-dependent efficacy in 2024 pediatric trial) but not systematically explored.

rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine::rich7::0.what_it_is_line: A plant extract from Rhodiola rosea roots, used as an herbal supplement for stamina and stress.
rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine::rich7::0.what_it_is: Rhodiola rosea is a flowering plant native to high-altitude regions of Europe and Asia. The supplement is made from its roots, which contain a mix of active compounds including rosavins and salidroside. People typically take it as a dried extract in capsule or powder form, often standardized to contain specific amounts of these active ingredients.
rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine::rich7::0.how_it_works_line: Modulates stress hormones and boosts cellular energy production, potentially improving stamina and mental resilience.
rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine::rich7::0.how_it_works: Rhodiola appears to work on multiple levels. First, it may dampen stress hormone pathways — animal studies show it reduces cortisol and related stress signals that wear down the body over time. Second, it likely boosts energy production in cells by enhancing mitochondrial function (mitochondria are the tiny power plants inside your cells). Third, it seems to calm inflammatory responses — reducing immune overactivation that contributes to fatigue, muscle damage, and sluggish thinking. The exact molecular pathways are still being mapped, but the compound appears to act as an adaptogen: a substance that helps your body resist and recover from both physical and mental stress.
rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine::rich7::0.safety_line: Well-tolerated in short-term trials; long-term and drug-interaction safety remain largely untested.
rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine::rich7::0.safety_detail: Trials lasting weeks to a few months reported few serious side effects; mild headache, dizziness, and dry mouth appeared occasionally in small samples. However, retrieved studies are limited in duration and population scope — most excluded older adults, pregnant women, and people with kidney or liver disease. Long-term safety (months to years of daily use) and interactions with medications have not been adequately studied.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety unknown: most trials last weeks to a few months; effects of daily use over years are unstudied.
Drug interactions untested: potential for interactions with sedatives, stimulants, and mood-altering medications has not been rigorously investigated.
Pregnant women, kidney/liver disease, and adolescents largely absent from trials — efficacy and safety in these groups remain unproven.
rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine::rich7::0.chem_meaning: Rhodiola's active compounds (rosavins, salidroside) are small organic molecules with moderate water solubility, allowing them to be absorbed from the gut and cross into cells and tissues. This makes the extract suitable for oral supplement form, though absorption varies and is affected by food and stomach pH.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies and systematic reviews (including a 2023 review of randomized controlled trials with n=263 total, and a 2025 RCT on punch explosive power in 96 untrained participants) found that Rhodiola supplementation showed improvements in physical performance metrics — though the effect sizes were modest and varied across studies. The 2025 trial tested Rhodiola combined with caffeine, while earlier reviews covered Rhodiola alone.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Three human randomized trials exist with consistent directional findings, meeting the threshold for Moderate. However, the total sample across studies (~369 participants) is still modest and limits precision — the true effect size could be somewhat larger or smaller than current estimates suggest.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human RCT (2015) found that Rhodiola extract reduced anxiety and stress symptoms. Two animal studies (2026 and 2020) showed that Rhodiola reduced stress-induced anxiety and cortisol levels in rodent models of chronic stress and autoimmune disease. These are promising early signals, but human evidence is extremely limited.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study exists, so consistency across independent human trials cannot be assessed. Animal data is encouraging but does not establish that the effect translates to people. This combination puts the outcome at Emerging — early promise requiring more human research.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human studies (a 2022 systematic review and a 2014 RCT in 24 runners) found that Rhodiola reduced inflammation markers and muscle damage after exercise. Four animal studies (2026, 2024, 2022, 2024) showed similar reductions in inflammatory biomarkers and immune activation in models of arthritis, diabetes, and stress. The human evidence is small in sample size (~34 verified participants), and a single systematic review carries the human findings without independent replication.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple study types (RCTs, systematic reviews) and both human and animal evidence point in the same direction, meeting Moderate. However, the human sample is modest (~34 participants across 2 verified studies) and there is only one meta-analysis — not independent replicated human trials — so precision and consistency are limited.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human RCTs (2025 trial on digital eye strain and cognition, and 2015 study on anxiety and cognition) found benefits to cognitive performance or cognition-related outcomes such as focus and mental clarity. Sample sizes could not be verified from the abstracts, so the total number of participants is uncertain.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two human RCTs provide directional support for a moderate effect on cognition. However, sample sizes are unconfirmed and modest, limiting precision. No animal studies were included, so the breadth of evidence is narrower than for other outcomes.

rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine::rich7::0.evidence_base: The evidence for Rhodiola is anchored in human studies — most outcomes rely on at least one RCT or systematic review of RCTs. Animal studies provide mechanistic support but are secondary. Trials are typically short-term (weeks to months) and involve younger, healthier populations (mostly excluding older adults, pregnancy, and chronic disease). Most human studies involved small samples (24–263 participants), which limits the precision of effect estimates. Recent studies (2022–2025) dominate the retrieved records, suggesting active ongoing research.
rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine::rich7::0.open_questions: The retrieved records show strong coverage of exercise performance and emerging data on stress, but cognition and inflammation rely on fewer independent human trials. Long-term effects (beyond a few months) are not represented in the sample provided. Older adults, people with chronic disease, and pregnant women are largely absent from the trials, so whether Rhodiola works or is safe in these populations is unknown. Whether effects vary by dose, extract standardization, or individual health status remains unclear from the current data.

selenium::clarity-engine::rich7::c1d7a63.what_it_is_line: Essential mineral your body needs for protein production and antioxidant defense.
selenium::clarity-engine::rich7::c1d7a63.what_it_is: Selenium is a chemical element (atomic number 34) that your body obtains from food and supplements. It is not made by your body — it must come from dietary sources like Brazil nuts, fish, eggs, or fortified grains. In supplements, selenium is available in several forms: selenomethionine (an amino acid that contains selenium), sodium selenate (an inorganic salt), or selenium-enriched yeast. People typically take it as a pill or capsule.
selenium::clarity-engine::rich7::c1d7a63.how_it_works_line: Acts as a core ingredient in proteins that fight oxidative stress and regulate immune balance.
selenium::clarity-engine::rich7::c1d7a63.how_it_works: Selenium works by becoming part of special proteins called selenoproteins — think of it as a building block that makes these proteins functional. These selenoproteins act as antioxidants: they neutralize harmful molecules called free radicals that build up in your cells and trigger inflammation and aging-like damage. Selenium also plays a role in thyroid hormone metabolism — the thyroid is a gland that produces hormones controlling metabolism, and selenium-containing enzymes help convert thyroid hormones into their active forms. Additionally, selenium influences how your immune system responds to threats: it helps fine-tune the balance between fighting infections and avoiding overactive immune responses (which can lead to autoimmune disease). The exact pathways vary by tissue, but the core idea is that without enough selenium, your cells lack key tools to defend themselves and regulate inflammatory signals.
selenium::clarity-engine::rich7::c1d7a63.safety_line: Generally well tolerated in standard supplemental doses; toxicity possible at very high intakes.
selenium::clarity-engine::rich7::c1d7a63.safety_detail: Most trials retrieved reported minimal side effects at recommended supplemental doses (typically 50–400 µg/day in adults). However, these studies were often short-term and enrolled relatively narrow populations. At very high intakes — well above normal supplementation — selenium can accumulate and cause toxicity (selenosis), marked by hair loss, brittle nails, and neurological symptoms. The safe upper limit for adults is around 400 µg/day, and individual tolerance may vary.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions unknown: no adequately powered trials retrieved examining selenium with major medications (anticoagulants, anticonvulsants, thyroid drugs); clinical caution advised.
Pregnancy and lactation: not adequately tested in these populations; excluded from most trials; use only under medical guidance.
Kidney disease: excluded from nearly all trials retrieved; selenium handling may differ in renal impairment — untested risk.
Long-term safety (>2 years): most trials were under 12 months; cumulative effects over years not established in the records provided.
selenium::clarity-engine::rich7::c1d7a63.chem_meaning: Selenium is a small, dense element (atomic weight 78.97) that exists as various chemical forms depending on the supplement. Selenomethionine is organic (contains carbon) and more easily absorbed by the intestine; inorganic selenate is water-soluble and less readily retained by the body. This difference in chemistry affects how much selenium reaches your tissues and how long it stays — one reason trial results can vary depending on which form is tested.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Fifteen human trials and 2 animal studies, converged across 3 independent meta-analyses, consistently show that selenium supplementation reduces thyroid autoantibodies (immune markers that attack the thyroid) and improves thyroid hormone control in autoimmune thyroid disease. A 2025 systematic review of n=1,610 patients with Hashimoto's thyroiditis found meaningful benefits; a 2026 RCT of n=430 individuals with newly diagnosed Graves' hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) showed selenium combined with other treatments accelerated disease control. Studies span 2016–2026, covering both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple independent meta-analyses and large RCTs with consistent results across different autoimmune thyroid conditions; adequately powered samples and 15 human studies provide robust evidence that this is a replicated, reliable finding.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twelve human studies and 11 animal studies (23 total) examined selenium's effects on memory, processing speed, and cognitive decline. A 2022 meta-analysis of n=1,350 patients with mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease found modest benefits; a 2018 meta-analysis pooling n=6,306 healthy mid-to-older adults showed smaller or unclear effects on maintaining cognition. A 2019 RCT in Alzheimer's patients (n=79) using selenium combined with probiotics reported improvements in metabolic markers. The animal data suggest selenium's antioxidant role may protect brain cells, but human evidence focuses mainly on disease populations rather than prevention in healthy people.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only 6 primary human studies and 3 pooled analyses (below the threshold for Strong tier); modest sample sizes in most cognitive trials and inconsistent results in healthy populations versus disease populations limit confidence. The mechanism is plausible, but human evidence is still gathering.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Ten human studies and 7 animal studies examined selenium's effects on immune responses and disease markers. A 2024 meta-analysis of n=2,381 multiple sclerosis patients showed modest immunomodulatory effects; a 2017 meta-analysis reviewing coronary heart disease (n=43,998) found selenium's immune-related benefits contributed to cardiovascular benefit. A 2017 RCT of n=23 older adults showed selenium both enhanced and sometimes reduced responses to influenza vaccine, indicating context-dependent effects. Systematic reviews from 2019–2021 examined selenium in HIV and other infections, generally supporting an immune-balancing role.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only 5 primary human studies and 5 pooled analyses (below Strong threshold); heterogeneous outcomes across different immune contexts (autoimmune disease, infection, vaccine response) make it difficult to draw one unified conclusion; quality evidence present but limited in breadth.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eighteen human studies and 11 animal studies (29 total) measured inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein, and other immune signals) in response to selenium supplementation. Four independent meta-analyses converged on a consistent anti-inflammatory signal with a pooled effect size (standardized mean difference) of −0.48 [−0.96 to 0]. Studies span endometriosis (2026 RCT, n=66), polycystic ovarian syndrome (2023 meta-analysis, n=389), Alzheimer's disease (2022 meta-analysis, n=1,350), and coronary disease (2017 meta-analysis, n=43,998). Over 47,000 verified participants across 13 of the 29 studies demonstrate broad evidence of reduced inflammatory markers across diverse disease states.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple convergent meta-analyses, large overall sample size, consistent effect direction, and replication across different disease contexts and populations provide strong evidence that selenium reduces inflammation as a general mechanism.

selenium::clarity-engine::rich7::c1d7a63.evidence_base: The evidence base for selenium is predominantly human (15 human studies for thyroid; 12 for cognition; 10 for immune function; 18 for inflammation), with supporting animal models. The dominant study types are meta-analyses and systematic reviews (reflecting accumulated RCT data), with recent trials from 2014–2026. For thyroid and inflammation, the body of evidence is large (>15 human trials each) and replicated across independent meta-analyses, raising confidence. For cognition and immune function, evidence is more limited (6–10 primary human studies each), with shorter follow-up periods and smaller individual trials. The recency of many trials (2022–2026) suggests active research, though the constraint that most trial abstracts omit sample size means the true total participant count is likely larger than the verified numbers.
selenium::clarity-engine::rich7::c1d7a63.open_questions: The records provided show strong evidence in autoimmune thyroid disease but do not include trials in hypothyroid individuals without autoimmunity, so whether selenium helps euthyroid (normal) thyroid function is not addressed here. For cognition, trials focus on diseased populations (Alzheimer's, mild cognitive impairment) with limited testing in cognitively healthy people — prevention efficacy remains unclear. Long-term safety and efficacy beyond 12 months are underrepresented; most trials run 3–6 months. Specific populations (pregnant women, children, people with kidney disease) are nearly absent from the retrieved studies, leaving their risk–benefit profile untested in these records.

sulforaphane::clarity-engine::rich7::377.what_it_is_line: Plant compound from broccoli that triggers cells to activate protective defense systems.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine::rich7::377.what_it_is: Sulforaphane is a small molecule (molecular formula C₆H₁₁NOS₂, weighing 177.3 daltons) found naturally in cruciferous vegetables, especially broccoli and broccoli sprouts. It forms when raw broccoli is chopped or chewed, released from a precursor compound called glucoraphanin. People typically consume it either by eating broccoli and sprouts, or as a supplement in capsule or extract form.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine::rich7::377.how_it_works_line: Activates a master switch protein that tells cells to ramp up their built-in detox and damage-fighting machinery.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine::rich7::377.how_it_works: Sulforaphane binds to and activates a protein called Nrf2 (a transcription factor — a cellular control switch that turns genes on and off). When Nrf2 is activated, it travels into the cell nucleus and switches on a suite of genes that encode detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins — substances that neutralize harmful molecules and reduce inflammation. This response also helps cells resist oxidative stress (damage from free radicals, reactive oxygen species that accumulate during aging and disease). Additionally, sulforaphane may dampen NF-κB, another control switch that typically amplifies inflammatory signals in the cell. The net effect is a coordinated boost to the cell's self-defense and housekeeping systems — essentially telling the cell to 'clean house' and reduce inflammatory noise.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine::rich7::377.safety_line: Mostly well-tolerated in short trials; long-term and drug-interaction risks remain poorly studied.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine::rich7::377.safety_detail: The human trials retrieved — mostly 4–12 weeks long — reported few serious adverse events and no major safety signals. Mild gastrointestinal side effects (bloating, nausea) and headache appear occasionally in supplemented groups, at rates similar to or slightly higher than placebo. However, trials were generally small (15–172 participants) and short-duration, and the population base remains narrow: most studies enrolled people with schizophrenia, autism, depression, or specific medical conditions. No adequately powered safety studies in healthy adults over months to years have been retrieved.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions untested: sulforaphane may modulate cytochrome P450 enzymes (the liver's drug-processing machinery); interaction with medications has not been systematically studied.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: excluded from virtually all trials; safety unknown.
Kidney disease: one trial (n=30, hemodialysis patients) showed sulforaphane did not meaningfully alter target gene expression; dosing and safety in renal impairment remain unclear.
High-dose supplementation: most trials used 50–150 mg daily; effects and tolerability at higher or prolonged doses are not documented in the records provided.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine::rich7::377.chem_meaning: Sulforaphane is a small, moderately lipophilic molecule (XLogP 1.4, meaning it is neither strongly water-loving nor fat-loving). This moderate lipophilicity allows it to cross cell membranes reasonably well and reach intracellular targets like Nrf2, yet it remains water-soluble enough for absorption in the gut. Its isothiocyanate group (the –N=C=S moiety) is the chemically reactive part that reacts with Nrf2's cysteine residues, forming a covalent bond that activates the protein.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human trials (and eight animal models) examined sulforaphane's effects on cognitive function and processing speed. Recent randomized controlled trials (2022–2025) in healthy older adults and patients with schizophrenia or autism found improvements in processing speed and negative cognitive symptoms when sulforaphane was added to standard treatment or given alone. A 2025 meta-analysis and systematic review synthesized multiple RCTs in schizophrenia. A 2023 double-blind trial in children with autism (design reported) and a 2022 trial in first-episode schizophrenia (n=172) showed measurable cognitive benefits. Verified sample sizes span at least ~238 participants across three studies; most abstracts do not report sample sizes, so the true number is substantially larger.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence rests on a single meta-analysis and several small-to-moderate RCTs, mostly in psychiatric populations rather than the general population. No independently replicated meta-analysis or large independent cohort study is in the records; consistency is not yet confirmed across different populations and research groups.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human trials examined sulforaphane's effect on depressive symptoms, negative mood, and mood-related outcomes. A 2021 RCT (n=66) in patients with depression and cannabis use history showed efficacy; a 2022 trial in healthy older adults reported improvements in negative mood and processing speed; a 2025 meta-analysis in schizophrenia (which includes mood and negative symptoms as outcomes) found overall benefit. Recent 2025 RCTs in schizophrenia patients (n=24, n=42) added sulforaphane to antipsychotics and measured mood and negative symptom improvement. A 2025 trial in former smokers and an open-label 2023 trial in fragile-X-associated tremor and ataxia syndrome also examined mood endpoints. Verified sample sizes exceed ~352 participants across six studies; most do not report exact n, so total is likely larger.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Efficacy is supported by a single meta-analysis and multiple small RCTs, primarily in schizophrenia and depression populations. The meta-analysis is not independently replicated; consistency across diverse patient populations and in primary prevention remains unconfirmed.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human studies and twenty animal models investigated inflammatory markers and immune responses. A 2025 meta-analysis (n=333) in autism spectrum disorder examined inflammatory markers; a 2024 RCT (n=30) in hemodialysis patients measured Nrf2 and NF-κB mRNA expression (a key inflammatory pathway); a 2025 RCT (n=42) in schizophrenia patients tracked inflammatory outcomes. Animal models (2019–2026) showed sulforaphane reduced liver inflammation, gut-liver axis dysfunction, and inflammatory injury in multiple disease contexts (sickle cell disease, Helicobacter pylori infection, toxic chemical exposure in fish). Human trials span psychiatric and medical conditions (schizophrenia, autism, dialysis, lung cancer risk); verified sample sizes total ~674 participants across six studies, with many abstracts omitting n.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Five primary human studies and two meta-analyses provide moderate evidence, but the human database is smaller than for cognition/mood and remains concentrated in psychiatric and chronic disease populations. No randomized controlled trials of anti-inflammatory effects in healthy adults were retrieved.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five animal studies (rodents and fish models, 2019–2026) examined sulforaphane's effects on liver damage, detoxification, and metabolic health. A 2019 study in a sickle cell disease mouse model showed sulforaphane attenuated liver damage and heme overload. A 2025 multi-omics analysis in mice revealed sulforaphane improved gut-liver axis function and reduced liver injury. A 2025 trial of a broccoli seed extract–producing probiotic combined with sulforaphane showed hepatoprotective effects. A 2024 study in fish (Cyprinus carpio) exposed to a toxic chemical found sulforaphane modulated stress parameters and liver metabolome. A 2025 analysis examined sulforaphane against Helicobacter pylori in mouse livers. No human trials of liver health outcomes were retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is entirely animal-based; no human randomized controlled trials or clinical observations of liver health outcomes have been retrieved. Animal models do not reliably predict human pharmacology and clinical efficacy.

sulforaphane::clarity-engine::rich7::377.evidence_base: The evidence base consists of 7–7 human trials per outcome (mostly randomized controlled trials, 2021–2025) and 8–20 animal/mechanistic studies. Human studies are concentrated in psychiatric populations (schizophrenia, autism, depression) and people with specific medical conditions (chronic kidney disease, cancer risk, fragile-X syndrome); few or no trials in healthy general adult populations for most outcomes. Meta-analyses exist for cognition, mood, and inflammation but are not independently replicated. Trial durations are typically 4–12 weeks; no long-term (6+ month) human studies were retrieved. This means confidence in efficacy is moderate — real signals are present and consistent within studied populations, but the depth and breadth of evidence do not yet reach the highest tier.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine::rich7::377.open_questions: The records provided do not include long-term (>12 week) human efficacy or safety studies, limiting understanding of sustained benefit or late adverse effects. Healthy, young adults are largely absent; nearly all human data come from psychiatric or chronically ill populations, so whether sulforaphane improves cognition or mood in otherwise well people remains untested in the records given. Liver health is studied only in animals, so translation to humans is an open hypothesis. Drug interaction studies, pregnancy/lactation trials, and large head-to-head comparisons with established treatments are not in the sample retrieved. Finally, optimal dose, bioavailability from food vs. supplement, and durability of the Nrf2 response with prolonged use are not systematically addressed.

thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine::rich7:.what_it_is_line: A 28-amino-acid peptide that mimics a natural immune-signaling molecule found in the thymus gland.
thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine::rich7:.what_it_is: Thymosin alpha-1 is a short peptide — a chain of 28 amino acids (the building blocks of proteins) — that is chemically identical or very similar to a molecule naturally made by the thymus, a gland in your chest that trains immune cells. The compound is usually given as an injection. It was first isolated from thymus tissue and is now synthesized in the lab; it's also known as thymalfasin or by its chemical identifier 62304-98-7.
thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine::rich7:.how_it_works_line: Appears to activate and balance immune cells, particularly T cells, which patrol for infections and abnormal cells.
thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine::rich7:.how_it_works: Thymosin alpha-1 is thought to work by signaling to T cells — a type of white blood cell that acts as your immune system's first responder. The peptide likely binds to receptors (docking points) on the surface of these immune cells, triggering them to mature, multiply, and become more effective at detecting viruses and bacteria. It may also help regulate inflammation by shifting immune cells away from an overactive or misdirected response toward a more balanced one. The exact molecular targets remain incompletely characterized, but in lab and animal studies it consistently enhances markers of immune activity and reduces excessive inflammatory molecules.
thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine::rich7:.safety_line: Mild to no adverse effects reported in trials; safety in long-term use, pregnancy, and kidney disease remains untested.
thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine::rich7:.safety_detail: The retrieved trials reported few side effects — mostly mild local reactions at injection sites or minor systemic symptoms — with no serious safety signals detected in the studies provided. However, these trials were typically short-term (weeks to months), often small, and did not systematically assess long-term tolerability or safety in vulnerable populations such as pregnant women, children, or people with advanced kidney disease.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety beyond several months of use has not been adequately studied in the retrieved records.
Use in pregnancy, nursing, and children is not documented in retrieved trials; status unknown.
People with severe kidney or liver disease were largely excluded from trials; tolerability in these groups is untested.
Potential drug interactions (especially with immunosuppressants or live vaccines) have not been systematically evaluated in the records provided.
thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine::rich7:.chem_meaning: Thymosin alpha-1 is a large, water-loving peptide (molecular weight ~3108, XLogP -24, meaning it strongly prefers aqueous environments). Its extreme hydrophilicity means it dissolves readily in blood but cannot cross cell membranes or the blood-brain barrier on its own — it must act via surface receptors. This is why it is given by injection rather than orally, and why it exerts effects primarily in the bloodstream and lymphoid tissues.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 meta-analysis of 706 patients with severe pancreatitis found thymosin alpha-1 improved immune markers and reduced infection risk. A 2024 meta-analysis of 329 patients with acute exacerbation of COPD showed immune enhancement. A 2023 systematic review examined 19 COVID-19 patients in moderate-to-critical condition and reported immune restoration. Additional pooled analyses (2020, n=1144 for Entecavir-treated hepatitis B patients; 2025 RCT in acute necrotizing pancreatitis, n=502) showed consistent improvements in immune function markers. Across these studies, the pooled mean difference in immune outcomes was 7.54 (95% CI 6.66–8.41), representing a moderate boost to measured immune parameters.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Fifteen human studies and nine animal studies were retrieved, but only 7 primary human RCTs and 4 pooled analyses met criteria — below the threshold for a Strong grade. The effect is consistent and clinically relevant, but the human evidence base remains limited in scope and scale.
