outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 meta-analysis of 706 severe pancreatitis patients showed thymosin alpha-1 reduced infection incidence. A 2023 systematic review of 19 COVID-19 patients in moderate-to-critical illness found viral clearance or reduced severity. A 2020 meta-analysis of 1144 hepatitis B patients on Entecavir showed fewer breakthrough infections when thymosin was added. A 2012 RCT of 552 patients with chronic hepatitis C non-responsive to interferon-ribavirin found addition of thymosin alpha-1 improved viral response rates. A 2025 trial in 330 acute aortic dissection surgery patients showed reduced infection incidence. Pooled risk ratio for infection across studies was 0.56 (95% CI 0.4–0.78), meaning thymosin-treated groups experienced roughly half the infection rate.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Twelve human studies and six animal studies were retrieved; only 6 primary human trials and 3 pooled analyses qualified — limited but consistent evidence. The risk reduction is substantial and observed across diverse infections (bacterial, viral), but the human trials remain modest in number and mostly in acute or high-risk illness contexts.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 meta-analysis of 706 severe pancreatitis patients showed thymosin alpha-1 reduced inflammatory markers (IL-6, TNF-α, CRP). A 2020 hepatitis B meta-analysis (n=1144) documented decreased inflammation. A 2025 trial of 330 acute aortic dissection surgery patients measured immune function and organ inflammation, finding reductions with thymosin treatment. A 2022 retrospective cohort of 95 COVID-19 patients and a 2021 observational study (n=19) showed anti-inflammatory effects. A 2023 unclassified report (n=19) on long-COVID sequelae found immune rebalancing and reduced inflammatory cytokines. Pooled mean difference in inflammatory biomarkers was −30.12 (95% CI −35.75 to −24.49), a meaningful reduction.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only 7 human and 5 animal studies were retrieved; just 3 primary human trials and 2 pooled analyses met quality criteria — well below Strong threshold. The effect direction and magnitude are consistent, but evidence is concentrated in acute illness (pancreatitis, COVID-19, surgery), limiting generalizability.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 open-label RCT provided early evidence of antidepressive effects in a small proof-of-concept cohort (exact n and design details not fully specified in the abstract title). Two 1985 RCTs (n=41 each) in cancer patients post-irradiation measured T-cell recovery and reported mood improvements as a secondary observation. A 2023 study (n=19) on long-COVID sequelae noted improved mood alongside immune restoration. A 2003 unclassified report examined anxiety and depressive symptoms in hospitalized patients; a 2006 animal study investigated immune-related mechanisms. Across the 5 human studies retrieved, sample sizes are small and effect estimates unstable (pooled n~101 across 3 studies with quantifiable data).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only 5 human and 4 animal studies were retrieved, with imprecision (modest sample sizes, high heterogeneity in populations and designs). The 2025 and 1985 trials show signal, but the evidence is preliminary and concentrated in acute or post-treatment contexts; generalizability to primary mood disorders is unknown.

thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine::rich7:.evidence_base: The evidence base comprises 15 human studies (mostly RCTs and meta-analyses) and 9 animal studies across immune outcomes, with smaller numbers for mood (5 human, 4 animal). Most human data come from recent meta-analyses (2023–2025) of acute illness populations: severe pancreatitis, COVID-19, hepatitis B/C, and perioperative settings. The pooled analyses suggest consistent moderate effects on immune markers and infection risk, but the underlying primary human trials remain modest in scale and context-specific. Recency is good (majority 2020 onward), but the absence of large, long-term preventive trials in healthy populations limits confidence in broader applications.
thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine::rich7:.open_questions: The retrieved records show thymosin alpha-1 studied almost exclusively in acute or immune-compromised populations (severe infections, critical illness, post-treatment recovery) — there are few or no trials in healthy, immunocompetent people or in primary prevention. Duration of follow-up in the retrieved studies is typically short (weeks to months); durability of effects and optimal dosing schedules remain unclear. The mood/depression evidence rests on small, heterogeneous samples from very different contexts (cancer survivors, COVID-19, hospitalization); whether thymosin alpha-1 has a genuine antidepressive effect independent of immune restoration or in primary mood disorders is an open question. The mechanism by which it modulates mood — whether via immune rebalancing, direct neurological signaling, or another pathway — is not established in these records.

vesugen::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73b.what_it_is_line: Experimental injectable peptide; human safety and efficacy unproven.
vesugen::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73b.what_it_is: Vesugen is a short protein-like molecule (peptide) designed for injection. It is not approved by regulatory agencies for human use and remains in early research stages. The compound is typically supplied as a research chemical and is not licensed as a medication; anyone considering use should understand it is experimental and its safety profile in humans has not been established through adequate clinical trials.
vesugen::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73b.how_it_works_line: Mechanism in humans unclear; animal/cell studies suggest vascular or tissue effects.
vesugen::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73b.how_it_works: Vesugen's precise mechanism of action in humans is not yet established. Preliminary research (primarily in cell cultures and animal models) suggests it may influence blood vessel formation or tissue repair pathways, but the specific molecular targets and signaling cascades remain poorly characterized in human biology. Without human studies, how — or whether — it actually works in people is unknown. Any description of its cellular actions at this stage is speculative.
vesugen::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73b.safety_line: No human safety data; unproven tolerability, side effects, and risks unknown.
vesugen::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73b.safety_detail: No adequately powered human clinical trials of Vesugen have been retrieved. There is no established safety profile in any human population. Injection of research-stage peptides carries inherent risks including injection-site reactions, immune responses, and unknown systemic effects that have not been studied.
safety_bullets: No human trial data: tolerability, adverse events, and dose safety completely untested in people.
Immune response unknown: peptides can trigger antibody formation or allergic reactions; no trial data available.
Drug interactions, contraindications, and exclusion criteria (pregnancy, kidney/liver disease, immunosuppression) have not been investigated.
Injectable research chemicals are unregulated; product purity, sterility, and authenticity cannot be assured outside licensed pharmaceutical manufacture.
vesugen::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73b.chem_meaning: As a peptide, Vesugen is a chain of amino acids and is likely too large and polar to cross cell membranes passively; it probably works by binding to cell-surface receptors or entering cells via active transport. Peptides are also vulnerable to breakdown by digestive enzymes and immune recognition, which is why it is administered by injection rather than orally.
vesugen::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73b.evidence_base: No human efficacy or safety outcomes are gradeable from the retrieved records. The compound has not progressed to clinical trials in any studied population. Published research, if any, is limited to preclinical (cell and animal) models. The evidence base is insufficient to support any clinical claim.
vesugen::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73b.open_questions: What does Vesugen actually do in human cells or tissues? Does it work at all in people, or only in lab models? What are its side effects, tolerability, and safe dosage in humans? Which populations (if any) might benefit, and which might be harmed? These fundamental questions have not been answered by human research.

vitamin b6::clarity-engine::rich7::2625c.what_it_is_line: Water-soluble B vitamin essential for amino acid and neurotransmitter metabolism
vitamin b6::clarity-engine::rich7::2625c.what_it_is: Vitamin B6, also called pyridoxine, is a small organic molecule (chemical formula C8H10NO5P) that your body cannot make on its own — you must get it from food or supplements. It exists in several forms in nature and in the body; the most active form is pyridoxal-5-phosphate, which acts as a helper molecule (called a coenzyme) for over 100 different enzymes. People typically take B6 as an oral supplement (tablets or capsules) or receive it from B6-rich foods like chickpeas, salmon, and potatoes.
vitamin b6::clarity-engine::rich7::2625c.how_it_works_line: Helps enzymes process amino acids, neurotransmitters, and homocysteine throughout the body
vitamin b6::clarity-engine::rich7::2625c.how_it_works: Vitamin B6 works by attaching itself to dozens of different enzymes — think of it as a helper tool that these enzymes need to do their job. One major job is breaking down amino acids (the building blocks of protein) and converting them into neurotransmitters like serotonin and dopamine, which regulate mood and nerve signaling. Another key role is helping your body process homocysteine, an amino acid that builds up in the blood — high levels are linked to cardiovascular risk, and B6 helps keep it in check. B6 also supports immune function and helps produce hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Because it is water-soluble (it dissolves in water, not fat), your body does not store large amounts, so you need regular intake from diet or supplements.
vitamin b6::clarity-engine::rich7::2625c.safety_line: Short-term trials show good tolerability; long-term safety and high-dose effects not fully characterized
vitamin b6::clarity-engine::rich7::2625c.safety_detail: The retrieved trials, which span pregnancy, premenstrual syndrome, and depression studies, reported minimal adverse events and generally mild or no side effects at supplemental doses. However, most studies were short-term (weeks to months), and the data come from relatively narrow populations (primarily women, often in pregnancy or taking oral contraceptives). Long-term safety, effects at very high doses, and safety in understudied groups (children, elderly, people with kidney or liver disease) remain incompletely characterized.
safety_bullets: Very high-dose B6 (>1000 mg/day over months to years) can rarely cause nerve damage (sensory neuropathy); standard supplemental doses (~25–100 mg/day) show no such signal in retrieved trials
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: studied in multiple trials, generally well-tolerated, but long-term developmental outcomes at high doses not tested
Drug interactions with certain medications (e.g., levodopa for Parkinson's, isoniazid for tuberculosis) reported in clinical literature but not systematically evaluated in retrieved trials
People with kidney disease, certain genetic disorders (like homocystinuria), or taking immunosuppressants should consult a provider; no adequately powered trials retrieved in these groups
vitamin b6::clarity-engine::rich7::2625c.chem_meaning: Vitamin B6 is a polar, water-soluble molecule (XLogP −0.9, meaning it loves water more than fat) with a phosphate group attached, which makes it highly charged and easy for the body to absorb and transport in the bloodstream. Its small size and water-loving nature mean it is readily taken up by cells and does not accumulate in fatty tissues, which is why the body needs regular intake and overdose is less likely than with fat-soluble vitamins — but also why deficiency can develop relatively quickly if intake drops.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Meta-analyses and systematic reviews spanning 73 studies (61 human, 12 animal) with over 95,000 verified participants show that B6 supplementation or adequate status substantially reduces the odds of B6 deficiency (odds ratio 0.63, 95% confidence interval 0.41–0.95). Studies include pregnant women (2006 meta-analysis, n=1646), patients with chemotherapy-induced hand-foot syndrome (2021 meta-analysis, n=1570), and women with breast pain/mastalgia (2025 meta-analysis, n=951). Six independent meta-analyses have independently converged on this conclusion, indicating robust consistency.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple large, adequately powered meta-analyses with consistent findings across diverse populations and clinical contexts (pregnancy, oncology, pain syndromes) provide strong evidence. The outcome is tautological — B6 supplementation prevents B6 deficiency — but the data confirm it works across real patients.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human and four animal studies examined whether B6 influences homocysteine levels and cardiovascular risk markers. A 1998 observational study of 80,082 women (Folate and vitamin B6 from diet and supplements in relation to risk of coronary heart disease) found associations between dietary B6 intake and heart disease risk. A 2003 RCT (n=90) measured plasma B6 forms before and after supplementation. A 2026 small unclassified study (n=14) reported that B6 antagonised specific receptors involved in blood pressure regulation (P2X3 receptors in the carotid body). A 2006 meta-analysis (n=1646) in pregnant women touched on cardiovascular biomarkers.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one meta-analysis (2006) synthesised this outcome; no independent replication of that synthesis was retrieved, so the evidence remains at moderate confidence. The mechanistic plausibility is strong (B6 metabolises homocysteine), but human evidence is limited to observational data, small RCTs, and case reports — not yet a large, replicated trial base.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human RCTs and observational studies (no animal studies retrieved) tested B6 supplementation for depression and mood. A 2026 RCT (n=267) reported that high-dose B6 reduced depression symptoms. A 2023 RCT studied B6 in college women taking oral contraceptives and found reduced depression symptoms. Earlier work includes a 1989 RCT (n=68) on premenstrual syndrome and a 1987 RCT (n=19) on platelet serotonin uptake and premenstrual tension. A 2025 meta-analysis (n=951) on mastalgia also captured mood-related outcomes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single meta-analysis synthesised mood outcomes, but no independent replication of that review was retrieved; evidence remains moderate. Most studies are small to moderate in size, focused on specific populations (women, often with contraceptive use or premenstrual symptoms), and mechanistic rationale is sound (B6 supports serotonin synthesis), but a large, independent trial replicating the effect in a general depressed population has not been identified in the records.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies (no animal studies) examined B6 for nausea and vomiting, predominantly in pregnancy. A 1991 RCT (n=31) reported that B6 was effective therapy for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. A 2023 meta-analysis synthesised pyridoxine supplementation for pregnancy-related nausea and vomiting. A 2002 case report on Ginkgo seed poisoning also appeared in the records but is not directly relevant to B6 efficacy.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only ~31 verified participants across one measured RCT; sample size is very small. A single meta-analysis exists but has not been independently replicated. The outcome is promising and mechanistically plausible (B6 supports neurotransmitter synthesis and may act on nausea pathways), but evidence remains preliminary — more robust, larger trials are needed to confirm.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five studies (three human, two animal) examined B6 and cognitive outcomes. A 2000 systematic review (n=371) on B6 in pregnancy touched on cognitive development. A 2024 observational study (n=55) in neonates with pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy noted cognitive outcomes. A 2025 unclassified study combined B6 supplementation with a dementia drug (rivastigmine) in an in-vivo model of Alzheimer's disease. Two animal studies (2024 and 2014) showed that dietary B6 improved cognitive and sensorimotor gating in rodent models of developmental impairment and enhanced vaccine efficacy in TB models, respectively.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single meta-analysis or systematic review exists, but no independent replication in the records; evidence is moderate. Human data are limited and come from narrow populations (pregnant women, neonates with genetic epilepsy, one Alzheimer's model), and most trials are small or observational. Animal data suggest B6 may support cognitive resilience in specific contexts, but translation to healthy human cognition or dementia prevention is untested.

vitamin b6::clarity-engine::rich7::2625c.evidence_base: The evidence base is dominated by human studies (61 of 73 across the strongest outcome, vitamin B6 deficiency), with multiple meta-analyses and systematic reviews confirming efficacy for deficiency prevention. For biomarkers, mood, and cognition, evidence is moderate: mostly observational or small RCTs, often in narrow populations (pregnant women, women with premenstrual symptoms, neonates with rare genetic conditions). Nausea/vomiting evidence is emerging and small. Studies span from 1987 to 2026, with recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses (2023–2025) providing modern synthesis. Confidence is highest for deficiency prevention; lower for prevention of chronic disease or mood disorders in general populations.
vitamin b6::clarity-engine::rich7::2625c.open_questions: The records provided show strong evidence in pregnancy, mastalgia, and deficiency prevention, but do not include large trials in other populations (healthy adults, elderly, people with diagnosed depression outside the premenstrual context, or those with cardiovascular disease). Duration of follow-up in most trials is weeks to months; long-term (years) cognitive, cardiovascular, or mood outcomes are not well captured. Whether high-dose B6 (>100 mg/day) offers benefit beyond adequate status, and safety at high doses over years, remains unclear from the retrieved data. The sample here represents ~40 abstracts per outcome; gaps visible in these records do not mean the field is unstudied, only that larger or more diverse trials may not have been retrieved.

zinc::clarity-engine::rich7::8859ff0fae.what_it_is_line: An essential mineral your body needs for dozens of enzyme and immune functions.
zinc::clarity-engine::rich7::8859ff0fae.what_it_is: Zinc is a metallic element (chemical symbol Zn) that your body cannot make — it must come from food or supplements. It is a cofactor, meaning it acts like a helper that allows hundreds of proteins and enzymes in your cells to function. People typically get zinc from meat, shellfish, legumes, and seeds; supplements are available as tablets, capsules, or as part of multivitamins.
zinc::clarity-engine::rich7::8859ff0fae.how_it_works_line: Enables immune cells to function, reduces inflammatory signaling, supports wound healing and protein synthesis.
zinc::clarity-engine::rich7::8859ff0fae.how_it_works: Zinc works as a prosthetic group — think of it as a key part of the lock — in over 300 enzymes throughout your body. In the immune system, it is required for the development and activation of T cells and B cells (the immune cells that recognize and fight infections). It also regulates inflammatory signaling pathways; when zinc is low, inflammatory molecules (called cytokines — chemical messengers that trigger inflammation) can become overactive. Additionally, zinc supports the synthesis of new proteins and stabilizes cell membranes, both critical for wound healing and maintaining barrier function in the gut. Deficiency impairs all these functions, so repletion can restore them.
zinc::clarity-engine::rich7::8859ff0fae.safety_line: Generally well-tolerated at typical doses; long-term high-dose use and specific populations remain inadequately studied.
zinc::clarity-engine::rich7::8859ff0fae.safety_detail: Clinical trials of zinc supplementation report tolerability comparable to placebo in short to medium-term use. However, most published trials are limited to weeks or months; chronic safety beyond 1–2 years is not well characterized in the retrieved records. Copper deficiency and neurological toxicity have been observed with very high intakes (>100 mg/day chronically) in case reports, though this risk is minimal at standard supplemental doses (8–30 mg/day).
safety_bullets: Pregnancy and lactation: zinc is essential for fetal development, but optimal supplemental doses in these populations are not established in retrieved trials — discuss with a healthcare provider.
Kidney disease: zinc is filtered and metabolized by the kidneys; people with severe renal impairment have not been adequately studied and may accumulate zinc — untested risk.

Drug interactions: zinc can reduce absorption of certain antibiotics (e.g., fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines) and iron if taken together; timing of doses is important and understudied in the records provided.

Adolescents and children: most trials involve adults or younger children with specific infections; long-term supplementation safety in healthy adolescents has not been formally tested in retrieved records.
zinc::clarity-engine::rich7::8859ff0fae.chem_meaning: Zinc is a small, positively charged metal ion (Zn²⁺) that is highly polar and poorly absorbed through the gut on its own — it binds to proteins and amino acids for transport. Different formulations (zinc gluconate, zinc picolinate, zinc oxide) have different bioavailability; this is why form and timing of intake matter. Because it is an essential mineral, it accumulates in body stores (liver, bone, muscle), meaning chronic excess can theoretically exceed toxic thresholds, though this is rare with typical oral supplements.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twenty-seven human studies and four animal studies show that zinc supplementation enhances immune markers and reduces infection incidence in various populations. A 2024 systematic review of zinc for acute and persistent diarrhea in children, and a 2019 review of zinc in atopic dermatitis, both found consistent benefit. A 2025 RCT in HIV-positive individuals showed zinc supplementation improved gut integrity markers and inflammation (Zinc Supplementation, Inflammation, and Gut Integrity Markers in HIV Infection). Studies span immune-compromised patients (HIV), children with infections, and adults with inflammatory skin disease; at least 1,158 participants were verified across 11 of the 31 studies, though the true total is larger because many abstracts omitted sample sizes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Three independent systematic reviews and meta-analyses converge on benefit, indicating replicated synthesis. The large, verified participant base and diverse populations strengthen confidence. Strong grade reflects consistency, adequately powered analyses, and human-focused evidence.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eighteen human randomized controlled trials (no animal studies) show that zinc supplementation lowers blood glucose by an average of ~10.86 mg/dL (95% confidence interval −14.74 to −6.98), based on a pooled meta-analysis. Studies include people with prediabetes (2022, n=265), type 2 diabetes (2023, n=70 and n=419), and adults with obesity (2024, 2023). The effect appears consistent across age groups and diabetes stages, with improvements in glucose control and antioxidant markers.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only a single meta-analysis and systematic review exists; this conclusion has not yet been independently replicated or verified by another team. Human-only evidence and moderate pooled effect size (rather than robust independent confirmation) hold this at Moderate. The evidence is meaningful but awaits validation from an independent synthesis.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twenty human studies and two animal studies demonstrate that zinc reduces inflammatory markers (pooled effect size hedges' g = −1.541, 95% CI −2.268 to −0.814, a large reduction). A 2024 meta-analysis of zinc for primary dysmenorrhea (n=739) and a 2020 review of zinc in acne both found zinc treatment lowered inflammatory biomarkers. A 2025 RCT in HIV patients showed improvement in inflammatory markers; a 2023 RCT in middle-aged women with overweight (n=42) showed similar anti-inflammatory effects. At least 1,127 participants were verified across 9 of 22 studies, though the true total exceeds this.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two independent systematic reviews and meta-analyses confirm the anti-inflammatory effect, indicating replicated synthesis. Large pooled effect size, consistent direction across diverse conditions (dysmenorrhea, acne, HIV, obesity), and adequate participant numbers support Strong grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human and five animal studies show zinc's role in gastrointestinal function and infection recovery. A 2024 systematic review found zinc effective for acute and persistent watery diarrhea in children. A 2025 RCT in HIV-positive individuals showed zinc improved gut integrity markers (likely a measure of how well the intestinal lining functions). Studies span infectious diarrhea (shigellosis, parasitic infections), diarrhea in children, and HIV-associated gut dysfunction. At least 2,465 participants were verified across 4 of 12 studies, though the true total is substantially larger.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only a single meta-analysis and systematic review has been synthesized; independent replication does not yet exist in the records provided. Human studies dominate (7 of 12), and evidence focuses on infectious diarrhea and barrier function. Moderate grade reflects credible but non-replicated synthesis and heterogeneous outcomes.

zinc::clarity-engine::rich7::8859ff0fae.evidence_base: The evidence base is predominantly human (52 of 74 total studies), with randomized controlled trials dominating recent work (2019–2026). Three strong outcomes (immune function, inflammation) each have at least two independent systematic reviews confirming benefit, a hallmark of replicated synthesis. Blood sugar and gut outcomes are supported by systematic reviews but await independent verification. The total verified participant count is at least ~7,000 across multiple populations (children, adults, immune-compromised, metabolic disease), though true totals are likely much larger because most abstracts omitted sample sizes. This recency and breadth of human data — especially replicated meta-analyses for immune and inflammatory outcomes — supports a Strong overall tier.
zinc::clarity-engine::rich7::8859ff0fae.open_questions: The records show strong evidence in immune function and inflammation but lack long-term safety data (most trials are weeks to months). Optimal doses, formulations, and timing for different outcomes are not systematically compared in the retrieved abstracts. Pregnancy, lactation, and severe kidney disease are notably absent from the trial populations, so safety and efficacy in these groups remain untested. Additionally, whether the gut/digestion benefit extends beyond infectious diarrhea (to conditions like inflammatory bowel disease) is not clear from the records provided — the evidence focuses heavily on acute infection and HIV.

alpha-gpc::clarity-engine::rich7::15f238.what_it_is_line: A choline compound derived from soy or fish; supports cell membrane structure and signaling.
alpha-gpc::clarity-engine::rich7::15f238.what_it_is: Alpha-GPC (alpha-glycerophosphocholine) is a naturally occurring molecule found in small amounts in foods like eggs and fish. It is a precursor to choline, a nutrient your cells use to build and maintain cell membranes — the outer layer that controls what enters and exits a cell. It is also involved in producing acetylcholine, a chemical messenger (neurotransmitter) in the brain that supports attention and memory. Alpha-GPC is sold as a supplement in powder or capsule form, and is sometimes used medically in Europe and Asia for cognitive and neurological conditions.
alpha-gpc::clarity-engine::rich7::15f238.how_it_works_line: Boosts choline availability to support brain cell membranes and acetylcholine production.
alpha-gpc::clarity-engine::rich7::15f238.how_it_works: When you take Alpha-GPC, your body breaks it down to release choline and glycerol — two building blocks. Choline is then transported into brain cells, where it serves two main functions. First, it becomes part of the phospholipids (fat-based molecules) that make up cell membranes, helping them stay flexible and functional. Second, it is used as a raw material to synthesize acetylcholine, the neurotransmitter that enables communication between brain cells and is critical for learning and recall. Animal studies also suggest Alpha-GPC may activate a receptor called α7 nAChR (a docking point for acetylcholine-like signals) and may influence immune-related cells called microglia in the brain. However, the precise mechanisms that lead to cognitive effects in humans remain incompletely understood.
alpha-gpc::clarity-engine::rich7::15f238.safety_line: Most reported side effects mild and infrequent; long-term safety data in humans remain limited.
alpha-gpc::clarity-engine::rich7::15f238.safety_detail: The trials retrieved — primarily a large 1994 Italian study (n=2044) of acute stroke patients and more recent smaller trials — reported that Alpha-GPC was generally well tolerated, with side effects described as rare or minor. However, these studies were relatively short-term and focused on specific populations (acute stroke, mild cognitive impairment); long-term safety in healthy individuals and across broader age groups has not been adequately tested in the retrieved records.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions: not systematically studied in retrieved trials; potential interactions with cholinergic medications (those affecting acetylcholine) unknown.
Pregnancy and lactation: excluded from all retrieved trials; safety in these populations untested.
Kidney or liver disease: not specifically evaluated in retrieved studies; dosing adjustments or risks unknown.
Adolescents: no studies retrieved; effects on developing brains unknown.
alpha-gpc::clarity-engine::rich7::15f238.chem_meaning: Alpha-GPC is a relatively small, polar (water-soluble) molecule derived from the phospholipid backbone, making it readily absorbed and distributed to tissues including the brain. Its chemical structure allows it to cross or approach the blood-brain barrier and to be broken down into smaller, active components (choline and glycerol) that cells can use directly.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2023 meta-analysis pooled 9 studies (3 human, 6 animal) and found a mean improvement of 1.72 points on cognitive measures (95% CI: 0.2–3.25). The largest human trial was a 1994 Italian multicenter study of 2,044 stroke patients, which evaluated mental recovery after cerebral ischemic events. More recent studies (2022, 2024) examined effects in mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease models in rats and humans. Animal studies generally showed improvements in memory and neuronal health in the hippocampus, a brain region critical for memory formation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Three human trials exist but the meta-analysis is a single source not yet independently replicated; most study abstracts lack detailed sample sizes, limiting precision of the pooled estimate. The consistency grade is held at Moderate because one systematic review exists but lacks independent verification. The signal is promising but not yet robust enough for a Strong rating.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies and one animal study examined stroke risk or recovery after stroke. The largest was the 1994 Italian trial (n=2,044) of Alpha-GPC in acute cerebral ischemic attack survivors, which assessed mental recovery as a marker of brain protection. A 2021 observational study (n=977, 10-year follow-up) examined associations between Alpha-GPC use and subsequent stroke risk. A 2023 meta-analysis synthesized these findings. Animal models (2017) showed that late treatment with Alpha-GPC increased hippocampal neurogenesis (new neuron formation) after injury.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The human evidence is sparse: two studies with available participant counts total ~3,021, but most study abstracts do not report sample sizes. One meta-analysis exists without independent replication. The grade is Moderate because there is consistent direction (suggesting potential benefit in stroke recovery/prevention) across human observational and trial data, but the number of trials is small and the precision limited.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human studies and five animal studies examined immune function. The 1994 Italian stroke trial (n=2,044) included immunological markers alongside cognitive outcomes. A 2022 unclassified human study specifically evaluated clinical and immunological effects of choline alfoscerate in mild cognitive impairment. Animal studies (1992–1994, 2022) explored mechanisms including protein kinase C activation and effects on microglia (immune cells in the brain) in rat models, suggesting Alpha-GPC may modulate neuroinflammation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only two human studies are in the retrieved record, and the 1994 trial's immunological data were not the primary focus. Animal studies show plausible mechanisms (protein kinase C signaling, microglia modulation) but translation to humans is unproven. The grade is Moderate because the signal is consistent across animal work but human evidence is limited and fragmentary.

alpha-gpc::clarity-engine::rich7::15f238.evidence_base: The evidence base consists of a mix of human trials and animal studies, with the largest human trial dating to 1994 (the Italian multicenter stroke study). A 2023 meta-analysis attempts to synthesize findings across cognition and stroke outcomes, but this is the only systematic review retrieved, so conclusions are not yet independently verified. Most studies are 10–30 years old, with a few more recent animal and small human trials (2022–2024). The human evidence is primarily observational or from older clinical trials; precise sample sizes are often not reported in abstracts, limiting overall statistical power.
alpha-gpc::clarity-engine::rich7::15f238.open_questions: The retrieved records show a concentration of evidence in acute stroke recovery and mild cognitive impairment; effects in healthy, cognitively normal older adults or younger people are not well represented. Nearly all trials are short-term (weeks to months); long-term use and safety over years are unknown from the retrieved literature. The mechanism by which Alpha-GPC improves cognition in humans remains incompletely specified — animal data point to choline availability, neurotransmitter synthesis, and immune modulation, but which of these drives human benefit is not yet clear. Note: this reflects only the ~40 abstracts retrieved per outcome; a complete literature search may reveal additional studies.

bcaas::clarity-engine::rich7::565d3d71a5.what_it_is_line: Three essential amino acids your muscles prefer to burn for quick energy.
bcaas::clarity-engine::rich7::565d3d71a5.what_it_is: BCAAs are three amino acids — leucine, isoleucine, and valine — that are among the nine amino acids your body cannot make itself, so you must get them from food or supplements. They are called 'branched-chain' because of their chemical structure (a forked backbone). You find them naturally in meat, eggs, dairy, and legumes; supplements are usually a powder or capsule containing all three in various ratios, often 2:1:1 (more leucine) or 1:1:1.
bcaas::clarity-engine::rich7::565d3d71a5.how_it_works_line: They signal muscle to build and repair, and fuel intense exercise directly.
bcaas::clarity-engine::rich7::565d3d71a5.how_it_works: BCAAs enter muscle cells and do two main things. First, they activate a pathway (called mTOR) that tells your muscle to grow and repair after damage — think of it as a growth signal. Second, they can be burned directly for energy during intense exercise, sparing other fuels and potentially reducing fatigue from a different pathway that depends on tryptophan (another amino acid). When you exercise hard, your muscles preferentially take up BCAAs, especially leucine, and this uptake may help limit the central fatigue (the brain fatigue) that comes from tryptophan accumulation during endurance work. Whether this translates to measurable performance gains in humans remains an open question.
bcaas::clarity-engine::rich7::565d3d71a5.safety_line: Short-term trials showed mild or no side effects; long-term safety and interactions remain untested.
bcaas::clarity-engine::rich7::565d3d71a5.safety_detail: The human trials retrieved (mostly 4–8 weeks) reported no serious adverse events or tolerability problems related to BCAA supplementation. However, all available studies were of short duration in healthy or cirrhotic populations, leaving long-term use and effects in other conditions (kidney disease, certain neurological disorders) largely unknown.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety (months to years) not established in any retrieved trial.
People with kidney disease: excluded from nearly all trials; risk of amino acid buildup untested.
Pregnancy and adolescence: no studies retrieved; not tested in these populations.
Drug/nutrient interactions: not systematically studied; use caution with medications affecting amino acid metabolism.
bcaas::clarity-engine::rich7::565d3d71a5.chem_meaning: BCAAs are small, hydrophilic (water-loving) amino acids that cross the blood–brain barrier more readily than some other amino acids, which is why they can theoretically influence central fatigue. Their small size and polarity make them well-absorbed orally and relatively easy for muscles to extract from the bloodstream.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human trial (2026, n=308) tested BCAAs combined with tryptophan or methionine on appetite and exercise-related outcomes; a parallel animal study examined recovery from tryptophan-induced fatigue. The human trial appears to focus on appetite control, while the animal work shows BCAAs may counter central fatigue in rodents. The single human study prevents assessment of consistency across independent trials.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study directly addresses exercise performance, and it is paired with animal evidence. A single human trial is insufficient to establish whether BCAAs improve performance in people.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two animal studies (2023 and 2020) show BCAAs improved muscle strength or attenuated muscle loss in aged mice and in mice exposed to angiotensin II (a molecule that causes muscle wasting). Neither study translates directly to human strength outcomes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is animal-only and does not reliably predict human muscle strength gains; no human trials were retrieved for this outcome.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human studies (including a 2021 meta-analysis and systematic reviews from 2022 and 2018) and two animal studies examined muscle damage markers and soreness after resistance exercise or trauma. One 2022 RCT found BCAAs did not accelerate recovery after sprinting; a 2008 RCT (n=41) reported improvement in recovery from minimally conscious states, a neurological outcome rather than typical exercise soreness. A 2021 meta-analysis pooled results across multiple resistance exercise trials, suggesting BCAAs may modestly reduce soreness, but the verified participant count (41 from one trial) is small, making the estimate imprecise.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects consistent human evidence (5 trials, including meta-analyses) but modest sample sizes and some inconsistency in outcomes; the effect on typical exercise soreness is real but not large or universal.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two meta-analyses (2026, n=1015, and 2022, n=1080) combined data on BCAAs in cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy, reporting a pooled risk ratio of 0.7 (95% CI 0.56–0.88), meaning a 30% lower risk of adverse outcomes. Individual human trials include a 2013 RCT on hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence, a 2007 case report on insulin resistance in hepatitis C, and a 2018 study (n=21) on hypoalbuminemia and sarcopenia in liver disease. Eleven animal studies span metabolic dysfunction, liver regeneration, and fibrosis; a 2026 animal study examined early-life BCAA exposure and metabolic effects. Total verified sample across human studies is at least ~2116 participants across meta-analyses and RCTs, though most abstracts omit size.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects a meaningful pooled effect in meta-analyses and consistent direction across human trials, but limited primary human evidence (one main RCT plus pooled analyses) and precision concerns due to small sample sizes in individual trials and reliance on abstracts.

bcaas::clarity-engine::rich7::565d3d71a5.evidence_base: Most evidence is human and comes from systematic reviews and meta-analyses on cirrhosis and post-exercise recovery, published 2007–2026; individual RCTs are typically 4–12 weeks. Animal studies (2020–2026) address muscle atrophy, metabolic dysfunction, and central fatigue. The human trials cluster in hepatology and sports medicine; broader populations and longer durations are absent. Overall confidence is moderate because meta-analyses exist for liver health and recovery, but individual trials are small and heterogeneous in outcomes.
bcaas::clarity-engine::rich7::565d3d71a5.open_questions: The records show no studies in children, adolescents, or pregnant people, and no long-term (>12 weeks) human trials. For exercise performance, only one human study is available, so we cannot tell whether effects are reproducible or consistent. For muscle strength, all evidence is animal; whether rodent strength gains translate to humans is untested. Recovery/soreness evidence is human but imprecise, with sample sizes below 100 in most individual trials. The liver health meta-analyses pool data well but rest on a small number of primary trials, and the clinical significance of the 30% risk reduction remains unclear in different liver diseases.

betaine::clarity-engine::rich7::7f825c50.what_it_is_line: A naturally occurring molecule in cells that supports energy production and cell signaling.
betaine::clarity-engine::rich7::7f825c50.what_it_is: Betaine (also called glycine betaine or trimethylglycine) is a small organic compound found naturally in cells and foods like beets, spinach, and seafood. Chemically, it is a derivative of the amino acid glycine, with three methyl groups (tiny carbon-hydrogen clusters) attached. People typically take it as a supplement in powder or capsule form, and it's also consumed through diet. It plays roles in cell energy metabolism and in regulating water balance inside cells.
betaine::clarity-engine::rich7::7f825c50.how_it_works_line: Helps cells produce energy and manages cell water balance; may reduce fatigue and inflammatory markers.
betaine::clarity-engine::rich7::7f825c50.how_it_works: Betaine works through two main pathways. First, it donates methyl groups (chemical tags that cells use to turn genes on and off and to make other important molecules) in a process called one-carbon metabolism — this helps cells build proteins and produce energy more efficiently. Second, it acts as an osmolyte, meaning it helps cells retain water and maintain their internal salt balance, which is especially important during exercise when cells are stressed and losing fluids. In animal studies, betaine has also been shown to reduce inflammatory markers (immune signals that indicate tissue irritation), though the human evidence for this is limited. How directly these mechanisms translate to the endurance and strength gains observed in human trials is not fully clear, but the consistency of findings suggests betaine does influence physical performance in measurable ways.
betaine::clarity-engine::rich7::7f825c50.safety_line: Short-term trials reported few side effects; long-term safety and effects in specific populations untested.
betaine::clarity-engine::rich7::7f825c50.safety_detail: The human trials retrieved reported good tolerability — few adverse events were noted in studies lasting weeks to a few months. However, most trials were relatively short (2–12 weeks) and enrolled healthy or athletic adults, so tolerability in children, pregnant women, people with kidney disease, or those taking multiple medications has not been adequately studied. One study in prediabetes noted no serious safety concerns, but the overall safety database remains narrow.
safety_bullets: Kidney disease: betaine metabolism depends partly on kidney function; untested in renal impairment — consult a doctor if you have kidney disease.
Pregnancy and lactation: no human trials retrieved; unknown safety — avoid without medical guidance.
Drug interactions: no specific interactions retrieved, but betaine affects one-carbon metabolism pathways; may interact with folate, B12, or certain medications — inform your doctor of use.
Long-term use: trials retrieved were 2–12 weeks; safety beyond a few months is understudied.
betaine::clarity-engine::rich7::7f825c50.chem_meaning: Betaine is a small, water-loving molecule (XLogP 0.5, meaning it dissolves easily in water and in body fluids). This makes it readily absorbed from food and supplements and allows it to move freely through cells and bloodstream. Its small size and hydrophilic nature mean it can cross cell membranes and interact with many metabolic pathways without needing special transporters, which is why it has broad effects on cell energy and osmotic balance.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Across 16 human trials and 37 animal studies (53 total), betaine supplementation improved endurance and exercise performance with a small-to-moderate effect size (standardized mean difference 0.36 [95% CI 0.03 to 0.69]). Recent studies include a 2024 systematic review of 317 participants showing chronic betaine enhanced performance, a 2025 RCT in cyclists demonstrating improved 60 km time trial performance and one-carbon metabolism, and several 2023 RCTs reporting gains in anaerobic power and CrossFit performance. Three independent meta-analyses converge on this finding, suggesting replication across different study groups.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple large systematic reviews in recent years (2024–2025) with consistent human evidence and a pooled effect that excludes zero, plus replication across independent analyses. Over 3200 verified participants across the retrieved trials.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human studies and 17 animal studies (22 total) examined betaine's effects on blood lipids. A 2021 meta-analysis found betaine *moderately increased* total cholesterol levels — an effect that is counterintuitive and warrants caution. A 2022 meta-analysis examined broader cardiovascular markers. A 2018 RCT of 27 people with prediabetes found metabolic effects but with mixed lipid results. Total verified participants across human studies: ~1093.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only 1 primary RCT and 2 pooled analyses in humans (below Strong threshold); human evidence is limited and shows an unexpected direction (cholesterol increase rather than improvement), suggesting the effect is modest and context-dependent.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight human trials and 3 animal studies (11 total) assessed strength outcomes, with a pooled effect of 0.47 [95% CI 0.04 to 0.89], suggesting a small-to-moderate improvement. A 2025 narrative review surveyed betaine and aging, finding mixed strength results. A 2024 systematic review of 317 participants noted chronic betaine improved strength markers. A 2023 RCT reported increased strength in CrossFit athletes. However, a 2020 RCT of 15 participants found *no* improvement in muscle hypertrophy or strength over 6 weeks, and a 2021 RCT of soccer players also showed inconsistency. Verified participants: ~391 across 4 of 11 studies.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Four primary human studies and 3 pooled analyses (below Strong); effect size is positive but confidence intervals are wide, and individual trials show conflicting results. Evidence suggests a modest benefit in some contexts (longer durations, high-intensity training) but not universal.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies and 23 animal studies (27 total) examined inflammatory markers. A 2023 meta-analysis of 277 participants found betaine reduced inflammatory markers in human trials. A 2025 narrative review on betaine and aging reviewed inflammatory evidence. A 2021 RCT in soccer players (n=15) and a 2014 clinical trial in short bowel syndrome also reported anti-inflammatory effects. Animal studies consistently showed reduced inflammatory markers (e.g., TLR4/NF-κB pathway downregulation). Verified human participants: ~578 across 7 of 27 studies.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only 2 primary human studies and 2 pooled analyses retrieved (below Strong); human evidence is sparse. Animal data is robust, but translation to human clinical anti-inflammatory benefit is not yet confirmed.

betaine::clarity-engine::rich7::7f825c50.evidence_base: The evidence is dominated by 16 human trials for endurance (the strongest outcome) and smaller numbers for strength, lipids, and inflammation (4–8 human trials each). Most studies are RCTs lasting 2–12 weeks and enrolled healthy or athletic adults; very few included older adults, women specifically, or people with chronic diseases. The field has seen recent activity (2023–2026), with three independent meta-analyses converging on endurance benefits. However, for lipids and inflammation, human evidence relies on fewer trials and pooled analyses, limiting confidence.
betaine::clarity-engine::rich7::7f825c50.open_questions: The retrieved records show that most endurance studies are in athletes or young healthy people; whether betaine benefits sedentary or older adults is unclear. For strength, the records show conflicting individual trials (some positive, some null) despite a positive pooled effect, suggesting the benefit may depend on training type, duration, or dose — but the abstracts provided do not isolate these moderators. For lipids, the unexpected finding (cholesterol increase) is striking but rests on limited human trials, and no mechanistic explanation is visible in the records. For inflammation, the records include mostly animal studies; only a handful of human trials were retrieved, so the evidence in people remains preliminary. Sample sizes are often omitted from abstracts, so true total participant numbers are likely larger than reported but cannot be verified from the data provided.

ca-akg::clarity-engine::rich7::0cf7eab3c.what_it_is_line: A small organic molecule and key metabolic intermediate; calcium salt form used as a supplement.
ca-akg::clarity-engine::rich7::0cf7eab3c.what_it_is: Ca-AKG (calcium alpha-ketoglutarate) is the calcium salt of alpha-ketoglutarate, a small water-loving organic molecule with the formula C₅H₆O₅. Alpha-ketoglutarate is a compound your cells naturally produce as part of normal energy metabolism — it's an intermediate step in the Krebs cycle, the central engine your mitochondria (the power plants in your cells) use to burn nutrients for energy. The calcium salt form is used in supplements, where it's taken orally as a powder or capsule.
ca-akg::clarity-engine::rich7::0cf7eab3c.how_it_works_line: Participates in cellular energy production; may reduce oxidative stress and support metabolic renewal.
ca-akg::clarity-engine::rich7::0cf7eab3c.how_it_works: Alpha-ketoglutarate sits at a crossroads in cellular metabolism. Your cells use it in the Krebs cycle to extract energy from food and generate ATP (the molecule cells burn for quick energy). It also serves as a building block for amino acids (the units that make up proteins) and nucleotides (the building blocks of DNA and RNA). Beyond energy, alpha-ketoglutarate is a cofactor — a helper molecule — for enzymes that regulate the balance between oxidative stress (harmful reactive molecules) and antioxidant defenses, a process called redox homeostasis. In animal models, supplementing alpha-ketoglutarate has been shown to dampen oxidative stress and improve arterial elasticity, suggesting it may help maintain the structural health of blood vessels. Whether these metabolic and protective roles, when enhanced by oral supplementation in humans, meaningfully affect aging, cardiovascular health, or muscle growth remains an open question; human trials are only just beginning.
ca-akg::clarity-engine::rich7::0cf7eab3c.safety_line: Mild gastrointestinal effects reported in limited early trials; long-term safety and drug interactions largely untested.
ca-akg::clarity-engine::rich7::0cf7eab3c.safety_detail: Trials have reported only minor gastrointestinal tolerability issues. However, the human evidence base is extremely small — only one ongoing clinical trial (n=120) directly addresses safety and efficacy in middle-aged adults. No large, long-duration safety studies have been completed, and interactions with medications, kidney disease, pregnancy, and other conditions have not been adequately studied.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions: unknown — no retrieved trials tested co-administration with common medications or supplements.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: no evidence; not tested in these populations.
Kidney or liver disease: untested — alpha-ketoglutarate is metabolized and excreted by these organs; safety in impaired function is unknown.
Long-term use: largest trial is ongoing; no completed long-term safety data beyond weeks to months.
ca-akg::clarity-engine::rich7::0cf7eab3c.chem_meaning: Alpha-ketoglutarate is a small, water-loving molecule (XLogP −0.9, meaning it favors aqueous environments). This polarity means it dissolves well in water and is unlikely to accumulate in fat; it is readily transported in blood and urine. The calcium salt form improves stability and bioavailability, allowing the compound to be absorbed from the intestine and delivered to cells.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human trial (2023, n=120, ABLE-intervention study) is currently underway, measuring biological age and cardiovascular markers in middle-aged adults receiving alpha-ketoglutarate supplementation. Two animal studies support the hypothesis: aged mice (n=10, 2011) given alpha-ketoglutarate showed improved arterial elasticity and reduced oxidative stress markers; ruminant studies (2026) examined growth and health outcomes. The human trial is ongoing and results are not yet complete.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study, not yet published with full data, addresses cardiovascular outcomes. Animal models show plausible benefits, but translation to humans is unproven. Small sample sizes and single human trial prevent a higher grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: The same 2023 human trial (n=120, ABLE-intervention study) is the primary human evidence, measuring biological age markers in middle-aged adults. Two animal studies (2011, n=10 aged mice; 2026, ruminant models) suggest alpha-ketoglutarate may improve redox homeostasis and general health markers related to aging. No completed human data on lifespan, healthspan, or validated aging biomarkers are yet available.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human longevity research cannot be completed quickly; one ongoing trial in middle-aged adults is insufficient to establish efficacy. Animal data is suggestive but does not predict human aging outcomes. Consistency across independent human studies is absent.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: The 2023 human trial (n=120) measures body composition and muscle markers as secondary outcomes in middle-aged adults. Animal studies (2026 ruminant, 2011 aged mice) examined growth performance and muscle-relevant parameters. Human results are not yet published; animal models show some support for growth-related benefits, but the mechanism and magnitude in humans are untested.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human efficacy data on muscle growth is incomplete. Animal studies are suggestive but do not directly translate to human muscle hypertrophy. Only one human trial, not yet complete, addresses this outcome.

ca-akg::clarity-engine::rich7::0cf7eab3c.evidence_base: The evidence base consists almost entirely of one ongoing human clinical trial (n=120, 2023, ABLE-intervention study) plus two animal studies from 2011 and 2026. No large randomized controlled trials in humans have been completed with published results. Animal models (aged mice, ruminants) show mechanistic plausibility — improved arterial elasticity, reduced oxidative stress — but these are not human outcomes. The narrow human sample and absence of independent replication mean all efficacy estimates are highly preliminary and may change when full results are published.
ca-akg::clarity-engine::rich7::0cf7eab3c.open_questions: The primary human trial (ABLE-intervention, n=120) is the only study retrieved addressing these outcomes in humans, and it is still ongoing; full results are not yet public. No studies examined Ca-AKG in older adults (>65 years), in people with cardiovascular disease or metabolic disorders, or over durations longer than several months. Whether the redox and arterial benefits seen in aged mice translate to meaningful health improvements in aging humans — and at what dose and duration — remains to be determined.

cartalax::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73.what_it_is_line: A short three-amino-acid peptide; synthetic, injectable, experimental compound.
cartalax::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73.what_it_is: Cartalax is a synthetic peptide — a short chain of three amino acids (alanine, glutamate, and aspartate) linked together. Amino acids are the building blocks your cells use to make proteins. This particular tripeptide is manufactured in a laboratory and is typically given by injection. It is classified as a research chemical, meaning it has not completed the regulatory pathway required for medical use in most countries.
cartalax::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73.how_it_works_line: Mechanism not established in retrieved literature; requires further research.
cartalax::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73.how_it_works: The specific biological targets and pathways by which Cartalax acts are not clearly established in the retrieved research records. The compound contains acidic amino acids (glutamate and aspartate), which are involved in cellular signaling and protein function, but the exact role of this particular peptide in human physiology remains unclear. Without evidence linking it to a defined cellular mechanism, any claimed effects would be speculative. Further research is needed to identify what cells or systems it influences and how.
cartalax::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73.safety_line: Limited safety data; injectable research chemical with few tolerability studies retrieved.
cartalax::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73.safety_detail: No adequately powered clinical safety trials of Cartalax were retrieved in the search. The compound is typically used only in research or experimental settings. Because it is an injectable research peptide with minimal human exposure documented in available literature, the full spectrum of side effects, tolerability thresholds, and long-term safety remain unknown.
safety_bullets: Injection risk: No data on injection site reactions, sterility protocols, or local toxicity.
Drug interactions: Untested; no trials examining interactions with other medications or supplements.
Excluded populations: No studies in pregnancy, kidney disease, adolescents, or immunocompromised individuals — safety in these groups is unknown.
Long-term effects: All available data appear to come from short-term or animal studies; chronic human use is not documented.
cartalax::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73.chem_meaning: Cartalax has a molecular weight of 333.29 and is highly water-loving (XLogP −4.9), meaning it dissolves readily in aqueous solutions and poorly in fats. This chemical property makes it suitable for injection and suggests it will not easily cross cell membranes on its own — it likely relies on specific transporters or receptors to enter cells. Its small size and charged acidic residues (from glutamate and aspartate) mean it will not accumulate in fatty tissues and will be filtered relatively quickly by the kidneys.
cartalax::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73.evidence_base: No gradeable clinical outcomes were identified in the retrieved literature for Cartalax. The available records do not establish efficacy for any human health outcome. Any research on this compound appears to be preclinical, in vitro (cell-based), or exploratory in nature. This indicates the compound remains in a very early stage of investigation and has not yet produced evidence sufficient to assess its clinical utility.
cartalax::clarity-engine-v2::rich7::1f73.open_questions: Because no human efficacy data were retrieved, the fundamental questions remain unanswered: Does this peptide produce any measurable effect in human subjects? If so, at what doses, and for which conditions? All populations, age groups, and clinical contexts are currently untested. The absence of defined outcomes in the literature suggests Cartalax has not advanced to the stage of formal human efficacy trials.

citrulline malate::clarity-engine::rich7.what_it_is_line: An amino acid compound that helps cells produce nitric oxide, a signaling molecule that relaxes blood vessels.
citrulline malate::clarity-engine::rich7.what_it_is: Citrulline malate is a combination of L-citrulline (an amino acid — one of the building blocks your cells use to make proteins and other molecules) bonded to malate (an organic acid). It's naturally present in small amounts in foods like watermelon, but supplements contain much larger doses. People typically take it as a powder or capsule, usually 30 minutes to an hour before exercise.
citrulline malate::clarity-engine::rich7.how_it_works_line: Boosts nitric oxide to widen blood vessels and improve blood flow, helping muscles get more oxygen and nutrients.
citrulline malate::clarity-engine::rich7.how_it_works: When you swallow citrulline malate, your body converts the citrulline into nitric oxide — a chemical messenger that tells blood vessel walls to relax and widen. Wider vessels allow more blood to flow to your muscles during and after exercise, delivering oxygen and nutrients more efficiently. Nitric oxide also helps reduce the buildup of lactate (a byproduct of intense muscle work) and may lower the amount of effort your nervous system perceives during hard exercise. Better blood flow and lower perceived fatigue are the reasons it's studied for athletic performance and recovery.
citrulline malate::clarity-engine::rich7.safety_line: Well-tolerated in short-term use; long-term safety and effects in specific populations remain untested.
citrulline malate::clarity-engine::rich7.safety_detail: Published trials report few serious side effects from short-term citrulline malate supplementation in healthy, mostly young and middle-aged adults. Mild gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, bloating) have been noted in some studies. However, trials are typically brief (days to weeks), enroll narrow populations (mostly trained or recreationally active people), and do not formally assess long-term safety.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety (months to years of continuous use) has not been systematically studied in retrieved trials.
Pregnant women, nursing mothers, and adolescents under 18 were excluded from or absent in the studies provided — effects in these groups are unknown.
Potential interactions with nitrate-containing medications or other arginine-metabolism agents have not been evaluated in the retrieved records.
People with severe kidney or liver disease were not enrolled in trials provided — safety in these populations is untested.
citrulline malate::clarity-engine::rich7.chem_meaning: Citrulline malate is a relatively large, polar (water-attracting) molecule, which means it dissolves well in water and is absorbed through the intestine but does not easily cross the blood–brain barrier. The malate component adds additional metabolic activity — it participates in the cell's energy-production cycle (the citric acid cycle) — which may enhance the supplement's effect beyond citrulline alone, though this is still being investigated.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 meta-analysis and several systematic reviews (2020–2026) examined exercise performance in resistance-trained and recreationally active adults. Pooled data across 25 human studies showed a small average benefit (hedges g 0.196), meaning people performed modestly more repetitions or work output after taking citrulline malate versus placebo. A 2021 meta-analysis of 137 participants specifically on repetition performance during strength training and a 2020 analysis of 206 participants on perceived exertion and muscle soreness both found modest improvements. Results were consistent in direction but varied in magnitude, and most individual trial sample sizes were small (n=10–20).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple meta-analyses and systematic reviews confirm a small benefit across diverse exercise settings, but individual studies are small and heterogeneous in methods and outcomes, limiting certainty about the true effect size and who benefits most.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 meta-analysis and 2021 meta-analysis (n=137) on repetition performance during strength training, along with several RCTs from 2021–2025, examined resistance-trained and recreationally active adults. A 2023 RCT found acute citrulline-malate supplementation increased total work in short lower-body isokinetic tasks. A 2025 RCT examined changes in resistance training performance and blood biomarkers after six weeks. Collectively, 17 human studies showed modest improvements in strength-related outcomes, though one 2021 RCT found it ineffective during aerobic cycling. Verified sample sizes range from ~10 to 137 per study.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Consistent direction of benefit across multiple meta-analyses and RCTs, but individual trial sizes are small and results vary, suggesting a genuine but modest effect that does not meet the threshold for Strong evidence.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2020 meta-analysis of 206 participants specifically examined post-exercise muscle soreness and rating of perceived exertion, finding modest reductions. Additional meta-analyses (2021–2022) and RCTs (2020–2026) evaluated soreness and recovery markers across resistance training and sprint tasks. A 2026 RCT tested acute effects on 100 m sprint performance in trained sprinters. Studies consistently showed small to modest improvements in perceived soreness and fatigue, and several reported faster lactate clearance (the body's ability to remove a fatigue byproduct). Twenty human studies were retrieved; verified sample sizes range from ~10 to 206.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple meta-analyses and systematic reviews support a small benefit on perceived soreness and exertion across diverse exercise modes, but heterogeneity in study designs and outcome measures, plus small individual trial sizes, prevent a stronger grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight human studies examined endurance capacity — including a 2021 meta-analysis on repetition performance, a 2026 RCT in older women (n=10), a 2025 RCT on resistance training performance and biomarkers, a 2021 RCT on aerobic cycling (which found citrulline-malate ineffective), and a 2019 RCT on post-exercise blood pressure in hypertensive adults. The evidence is mixed: some studies support modest improvements in lower-limb endurance and work capacity, while at least one found no effect on aerobic cycling. Verified sample sizes are small (n=10–137 where reported).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Limited number of primary endurance studies (5 standalone trials plus 2 pooled analyses) and inconsistent findings between aerobic and resistance endurance tasks, combined with small and heterogeneous populations, place this below the threshold for Strong evidence.

citrulline malate::clarity-engine::rich7.evidence_base: The evidence base comprises 25–20 human studies, mostly RCTs and meta-analyses published between 2019 and 2026, with a small number of animal studies also retrieved. Most trials are relatively short-term (acute dosing or 6 weeks), enroll trained or recreationally active adults, and measure strength, power, or soreness via standardized protocols. Verified sample sizes in published abstracts range from ~10 to 206, though the true total across all retrieved studies is larger. No large, long-term trials in diverse populations (e.g., older adults, clinical populations) were identified in the records provided.
citrulline malate::clarity-engine::rich7.open_questions: The provided records show that citrulline malate has been tested primarily in young to middle-aged, trained or recreationally active people; older adults, sedentary individuals, and people with chronic disease are nearly absent from the sample. All outcomes rely on short-term supplementation (days to weeks); no study in the records examined chronic use over months or years. Effects in specific exercise modalities are inconsistent — aerobic cycling, for instance, showed no benefit in one trial — suggesting that the benefit may be context-dependent, but the records do not fully clarify when and in whom it works best.

coq10::clarity-engine::rich7::4d5406a88d.what_it_is_line: Fat-soluble molecule that cells use to generate energy; found in all living things.
coq10::clarity-engine::rich7::4d5406a88d.what_it_is: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10, also called ubiquinone or ubidecarenone) is a small fat-soluble molecule your cells naturally produce. It lives primarily in the energy-generating structures inside cells called mitochondria — think of it as a worker on an assembly line that helps convert the food you eat into usable energy (ATP, the currency your cells spend for work). Your body makes less CoQ10 as you age, and certain medications, especially statins (which lower cholesterol), can lower your levels further. It's available as an oral supplement in capsules or tablets, typically derived from fermentation or chemical synthesis.
coq10::clarity-engine::rich7::4d5406a88d.how_it_works_line: Shuttles electrons in cell energy production; protects cells from oxidative damage.
coq10::clarity-engine::rich7::4d5406a88d.how_it_works: CoQ10 works in two main ways. First, it acts as an electron shuttle in the mitochondrial energy pipeline — it ferries electrons between protein complexes, a critical step that allows your cells to efficiently generate ATP (the energy molecule they burn for every task). Second, it's a potent antioxidant, meaning it neutralizes harmful byproducts (called free radicals) that accumulate during energy production and can damage cell membranes and DNA if left unchecked. This dual role — energy production plus cellular protection — may explain why it affects so many health outcomes. Because CoQ10 is highly fat-soluble (XLogP 19.4, meaning it strongly prefers fatty environments), it embeds itself in the fatty membranes that wrap your cells and mitochondria, where it's positioned to do its work.
coq10::clarity-engine::rich7::4d5406a88d.safety_line: Generally well-tolerated in short-term trials; long-term safety and drug interactions not well studied.
coq10::clarity-engine::rich7::4d5406a88d.safety_detail: The retrieved trials — mostly 4–12 weeks in duration — reported few or mild side effects (gastrointestinal upset being most common); no serious adverse events were attributed to CoQ10 in the studies provided. However, all trials were short, none assessed long-term exposure (months to years), and most enrolled narrow populations (e.g., statin-treated patients, athletes, specific disease groups). The true safety profile in diverse populations and over longer durations remains unknown.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety: no trials >12 weeks retrieved; extended use in the general population is untested.
Drug interactions: CoQ10 is highly lipophilic and may interact with medications or other supplements that rely on fat absorption; not adequately studied in retrieved trials.
Excluded or underrepresented populations: no trials in pregnancy, adolescents, or severe kidney/liver disease; safety in these groups is unknown.
Statin interactions: some evidence suggests CoQ10 may mitigate statin-induced muscle symptoms, but the mechanism and optimal dosing strategy remain unclear.
coq10::clarity-engine::rich7::4d5406a88d.chem_meaning: CoQ10 is a large, highly lipophilic (fat-loving) molecule with a long hydrocarbon tail (10 isoprene units in the decamethyltetraconta backbone) and a quinone head-group. Its extreme lipophilicity (XLogP 19.4) means it dissolves poorly in water but readily embeds in fatty cell membranes and mitochondrial cristae, where its biochemical work occurs — this is why oral absorption depends on dietary fat and why formulation (powder vs. ubiquinone vs. ubiquinol) affects bioavailability.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converged on a cardiovascular benefit, with a pooled effect of a 0.96-unit reduction in a composite cardiovascular risk score (95% CI: −1.88 to −0.03). Human evidence dominates (16 human trials vs. 10 animal studies out of 26 total); verified participant count across 6 trials was ~3,364, though most abstracts omitted sample sizes, so the true total is substantially larger. Studies ranged from 2016–2025 and included statin-treated patients, burn patients, soccer players, and those with prediabetes/type 2 diabetes, with durations typically 4–12 weeks.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong human evidence (16 trials) with independent replication of findings across 4 separate meta-analyses, plus adequately powered pooled analyses, meets the threshold for Strong. Cardiovascular outcomes are directly measured and clinically relevant.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human trials and two animal studies examined lipid profiles. A meta-analysis of 2,794 participants found CoQ10 supplementation reduced LDL cholesterol and triglycerides in adults, and a 2026 cardiovascular meta-analysis included lipid markers in prediabetes/type 2 diabetes populations. Individual RCTs (n=30–104) in hypertensive, hypercholesterolemic, and metabolic syndrome patients showed improvements in lipid profiles. One observational study assessed dietary CoQ10 intake in familial hypercholesterolemia. Verified participant count across 3 studies was ~2,928, with most trials 4–12 weeks in duration.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate: only 3 primary human RCTs and 2 pooled analyses retrieved — below the number required for Strong. Evidence exists and is human-based, but the synthesis is smaller and less independently replicated than cardiovascular outcomes.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converged on an anti-inflammatory effect, with a pooled mean reduction of 0.45 units in inflammatory markers (95% CI: −0.67 to −0.24). Human trials dominate the evidence (16 human vs. 22 animal studies out of 38 total). Verified participant count across 7 trials was ~2,125, though most abstracts omitted sizes. A 2023 meta-analysis of 1,517 participants assessed optimal dosing; a 2020 review pooled oxidative stress parameters; a 2017 review (n=428) examined inflammatory markers. Recent studies (2023–2026) included juvenile idiopathic arthritis (n=58) and various chronic disease populations, with typical durations of 4–12 weeks.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong: 16 human trials with independently replicated findings across 5 meta-analyses, adequately powered pooled estimates, and direct measurement of inflammatory biomarkers (e.g., CRP, TNF-α, IL-6) meet the criteria for Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nineteen human trials and 5 animal studies examined muscle strength and physical function. A 2023 scoping review synthesized evidence on CoQ10 for sarcopenia, frailty, and falls. Individual RCTs included small samples: n=10–38 participants with multiple sclerosis, high-intensity training adaptations, chronic kidney disease, and statin-treated patients. A 2022 RCT (n=37) was double-blinded placebo-controlled in statin users; a 2023 RCT (n=25) was a crossover design; most durations were 8 weeks or less. Verified participant count across 8 trials was ~284.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate: 19 human trials exist, but only a single meta-analysis/systematic review was retrieved, and it has not been independently replicated — the consistency criterion for Strong is not met. Small sample sizes and short durations limit precision.

coq10::clarity-engine::rich7::4d5406a88d.evidence_base: CoQ10 has been extensively studied, with 26–38 trials retrieved per outcome. Human evidence predominates (16 human trials for cardiovascular and inflammation; 19 for muscle strength), supported by animal mechanistic studies. Most trials are RCTs ranging from 2016–2026, typically 4–12 weeks in duration, conducted in disease or aging populations (statin-treated patients, diabetes, arthritis, athletes). Four independent meta-analyses converge on cardiovascular and inflammation outcomes, lending credibility; lipids and muscle strength are supported by smaller or less-replicated syntheses. The recency and breadth of human RCTs is a strength; the brevity of follow-up (≤12 weeks) and the exclusion of many populations (healthy young adults, pregnancy, severe organ disease) limit what we know about long-term efficacy and broader applicability.
coq10::clarity-engine::rich7::4d5406a88d.open_questions: The records provided show no long-term trials (>12 weeks) — whether benefits persist or accumulate over months is unknown. Optimal dosing varies across studies (50–600 mg/day retrieved), but the records show only one analysis explicitly addressing dose–response. Populations in the retrieved trials skew toward older, disease-afflicted, or athletic cohorts; efficacy in healthy young adults or children is not represented in the sample. The mechanism of lipid lowering appears less consistent across studies than cardiovascular or inflammatory outcomes, suggesting moderating factors (diet, baseline lipids, dosage, formulation) that the records do not clearly delineate.

dhea::clarity-engine::rich7::b9bbdd8100.what_it_is_line: A steroid hormone your body naturally makes; sold as a supplement to raise levels that decline with age.
