Six independent meta-analyses or systematic reviews exist, particularly for blood sugar and lipids, indicating organized synthesis and replication in the field. Animal models (mostly rodents and cell culture) provide mechanistic support and generally precede human trials. The largest pooled sample sizes are in blood sugar (>1056 verified, likely 2000+) and lipids (>1768 verified). Trials typically run 4–12 weeks; only a few extend beyond 24 weeks. This suggests good short-term evidence for metabolic outcomes, but long-term durability remains largely unknown.
resveratrol::clarity-engine::rich7::e8da.open_questions: The records provided show human trials are concentrated in people with metabolic dysfunction (type 2 diabetes, obesity, metabolic syndrome, COPD); healthy populations are underrepresented. Bone health evidence includes mostly postmenopausal women and obese men — other age groups and sexes are sparse. Most trials last weeks to a few months; whether benefits persist or accumulate over years has not been adequately tested in the records given. Weight loss evidence is inconsistent across trials, and the records do not reveal clear predictors of responders vs. non-responders. Dosage, bioavailability, and formulation variations are mentioned in some abstracts but not systematically compared.

semax::clarity-engine::rich7::619afd6a79.what_it_is_line: Synthetic peptide derived from ACTH hormone; injected; studied for brain recovery.
semax::clarity-engine::rich7::619afd6a79.what_it_is: Semax is a short synthetic peptide — a chain of seven amino acids (the building blocks of proteins). It is derived from ACTH, a natural hormone your brain and body make. The exact sequence is ACTH (4-7), also called Pro-Gly-Pro, meaning it contains the amino acids proline, glycine, and proline in a specific order. People typically inject it subcutaneously (under the skin) or intranasally (as a nasal spray). It is often used as a research chemical and is not approved by major regulatory agencies like the FDA.
semax::clarity-engine::rich7::619afd6a79.how_it_works_line: Appears to activate opioid and melanocortin pathways in the brain; exact human mechanism unclear.
semax::clarity-engine::rich7::619afd6a79.how_it_works: Semax appears to work through two main routes in the brain. First, it targets opioid receptors — docking sites on brain cells that normally bind natural pain-relief molecules — especially one called the μ opioid receptor. Second, it activates melanocortin pathways, which are signaling systems the brain uses to regulate stress, mood, and nerve cell growth. In animal studies, when semax binds these receptors, it triggers a cascade of events: brain cells increase production of growth factors (BDNF and NGF), molecules that help nerve cells survive and form new connections, and they also reduce inflammation — the harmful swelling that follows brain injury. Whether these exact mechanisms operate the same way in human brains remains untested.
semax::clarity-engine::rich7::619afd6a79.safety_line: Short-duration trials reported no serious adverse events; long-term safety and interactions untested.
semax::clarity-engine::rich7::619afd6a79.safety_detail: The human studies retrieved were observational or short-term clinical trials, mostly conducted 15–25 years ago, and reported tolerability without detailed adverse event data. No serious harms were flagged in the records provided. However, these studies were small (14–73 participants), typically brief, and did not systematically screen for side effects or drug interactions. Long-term safety in humans has not been adequately studied.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions: unknown; peptide may interact with opioid medications or antidepressants — untested in retrieved trials.
Excluded populations: no adequate data in children, adolescents, pregnant individuals, or those with kidney or liver disease.
Injection/nasal administration risks: local irritation, infection, or immune responses possible but not systematically characterized in humans.
Research chemical status: Semax is not FDA-approved and purity/sterility standards vary by supplier — quality control is a practical unknown.
semax::clarity-engine::rich7::619afd6a79.chem_meaning: Semax is a hydrophilic (water-loving) peptide with an XLogP of −2.8, meaning it dissolves readily in water but poorly in lipid membranes. This property makes it unlikely to cross the blood–brain barrier — the protective shield around the brain — on its own. Intranasal delivery (nasal spray) bypasses this barrier by allowing the peptide to reach brain tissue directly through the olfactory nerve. Its 813.9 dalton molecular weight is relatively small for a peptide but still large enough that oral absorption would be minimal.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four animal studies (conducted 2008–2025) examined semax's effects on memory and learning in rats. They reported that semax increased production of brain growth factors (BDNF and NGF) in the hippocampus and frontal cortex — brain regions critical for memory — and protected against memory impairment induced by heavy metals. One 2025 study identified a molecular mechanism: semax targets the μ opioid receptor gene to enhance cellular recovery. No human cognition trials were retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence is from animal models, which do not reliably predict human cognitive outcomes. Translation to humans has not been tested.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human studies (RCTs and observational trials, n=14–73, conducted 1999–2018) and 28 animal studies examined semax in ischemic stroke and brain injury. Human trials reported improvement in neurological symptoms, recovery of vision in optic nerve damage, and reduced disease progression in post-stroke patients; a 2018 trial (n=67) specifically assessed efficacy at different stroke stages. Animal studies confirmed semax reduced brain cell death and inflammation after stroke. Across studies, mechanisms involved increased growth factor expression, reduced oxidative stress, and improved blood flow. Sample sizes in human trials were small and most older studies; a 2018 fMRI study (n=14) showed semax altered large-scale brain network activity (default mode network).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate: human evidence exists (6 trials, ~154 participants verified) with consistent direction (improvement reported), but no pooled analysis confirms agreement, trials are small and mostly observational or short-term, and precision is limited by incomplete reporting of sample sizes across the full literature.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight animal studies (2010–2025) examined semax's effects on mood-related behaviors in rodents. They reported that semax reduced depression-like and anxiety-like behaviors in rats exposed to stress, early-life trauma, or inflammatory challenges. Studies showed semax increased brain levels of mood-regulating neurotransmitters and growth factors, and corrected gene expression patterns linked to stress resilience. One 2021 study found semax attenuated both behavioral depression and neurochemical imbalance in rats with a history of early stress. No human mood or depression trials were retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence is from animal models. Whether these mood effects translate to humans has not been tested.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twenty animal studies (2014–2021) examined semax's effects on stress and anxiety responses in rodents. Findings showed semax reduced anxiety-like behaviors in stressed rats, lowered stress hormone levels, and altered immune markers (cytokines) associated with stress. Studies in rats under social stress, restraint stress, or neonatal adversity reported improvements in behavior and normalization of biochemical stress responses. One 2020 study found semax changed the composition of gut bacteria in stressed rats, a potential mechanism linking peptide treatment to stress resilience. No human anxiety or stress trials were retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence is from animals. Human efficacy in stress or anxiety disorders has not been tested.

semax::clarity-engine::rich7::619afd6a79.evidence_base: Semax has the most robust evidence for stroke and brain ischemia recovery, with 6 human trials (~154 participants; mostly observational or small RCTs, 1999–2018) plus 28 animal studies showing consistent neuroprotective effects. All other outcomes (cognition, mood, stress/anxiety) rest entirely on animal studies (4–20 studies each, 2008–2025). Human trials are small, mostly observational, and do not employ modern randomization or blinding standards. The literature is heavily weighted toward animal mechanistic work, which shows promise but does not reliably predict human outcomes. Recency varies; human trials are 15–25 years old; animal work is recent (2020–2025), reflecting renewed interest.
semax::clarity-engine::rich7::619afd6a79.open_questions: The retrieved human trials are small and lack pooled analysis or pre-registered protocols; it is unclear whether the reported stroke benefits are robust or reflect publication bias. Animal studies dominate; no human trials exist for cognition, mood, or anxiety — these remain untested hypotheses in people. Pediatric, geriatric, and pregnancy populations appear entirely absent from the retrieved records. Long-term safety (beyond weeks) and interaction with standard medications (anticoagulants, antidepressants) are not documented in the records provided. Whether intranasal delivery consistently reaches brain tissue at therapeutic doses in humans is an open mechanistic question.

tart cherry::clarity-engine::rich7::0f8a.what_it_is_line: A tart cherry extract or juice rich in anthocyanins, compounds that give the fruit its deep red color.
tart cherry::clarity-engine::rich7::0f8a.what_it_is: Tart cherry (Prunus cerasus) is a small, dark red fruit native to western Asia. People typically consume it as a juice concentrate, powdered extract, or whole juice. The active compounds are anthocyanins — pigment molecules that have anti-inflammatory properties — along with other polyphenols (plant chemicals with antioxidant effects). Most research uses Montmorency varieties, the most common commercial tart cherry.
tart cherry::clarity-engine::rich7::0f8a.how_it_works_line: Reduces inflammatory signals in the body by suppressing immune molecules that trigger pain and swelling.
tart cherry::clarity-engine::rich7::0f8a.how_it_works: Tart cherry anthocyanins reduce levels of inflammatory cytokines — signaling molecules that your immune system uses to amplify inflammation. They appear to work partly by inhibiting enzymes called COX and NF-κB, which are the biochemical 'switches' that turn up inflammatory responses. This is why it matters for exercise: after intense physical work, muscle fibers develop micro-tears; inflammation is the body's repair signal, but excessive inflammation causes the soreness (DOMS) and fatigue you feel. By muting that inflammatory cascade, tart cherry may allow recovery to proceed faster and with less discomfort. The mechanism has been shown in cell and animal studies; human trials measure whether that translates to measurable changes in blood markers and symptoms.
tart cherry::clarity-engine::rich7::0f8a.safety_line: Short-term use well tolerated in most adults; long-term and special-population safety remain largely untested.
tart cherry::clarity-engine::rich7::0f8a.safety_detail: Most studies reported no serious adverse events in adult participants over intervention periods of 1–14 days. Mild gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, diarrhea) occurred occasionally but rarely forced withdrawal. However, the trials provided were mostly short-term and enrolled relatively healthy adults; pregnant individuals, children, and people with kidney disease or on anticoagulants were largely absent from the records.
safety_bullets: Anticoagulant interaction unknown: tart cherry may have mild antiplatelet effects; untested in people on warfarin or other blood thinners.
Pregnancy and lactation: no adequate human studies retrieved; safety for the fetus/infant is unknown.
Kidney disease: excluded or not reported in most trials; no data on safety in impaired renal function.
Drug metabolism: anthocyanins may affect CYP3A4 enzyme; interactions with medications metabolized this way are not established.
tart cherry::clarity-engine::rich7::0f8a.chem_meaning: Anthocyanins are water-soluble pigment molecules (flavonoids) with moderate molecular weight (~300 Da). Their chemical structure allows them to cross cell membranes and reach immune cells, but they are also readily absorbed by the gut and rapidly metabolized by the liver and microbiota, which limits their systemic half-life to a few hours. This means repeated dosing is needed to maintain blood levels.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seventeen human trials, primarily RCTs comparing tart cherry juice or powder to placebo or control in athletes after strenuous exercise, found a pooled reduction in muscle soreness and recovery time (effect size −0.44, meaning a small-to-modest benefit). Meta-analyses from 2021 and 2026 converged on this outcome. Participants included runners, cyclists, and resistance-trained adults; soreness was measured by self-report or strength loss over 24–72 hours post-exercise.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence is direct and consistent across multiple systematic reviews, but statistical inconsistency between studies and a modest effect size held the grade at Moderate rather than Strong. The pooled confidence interval just touches zero, indicating borderline precision.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine human RCTs assessed whether tart cherry improves endurance or repeated-sprint performance; meta-analyses (2020, 2021) found a pooled benefit (effect size −0.53, indicating modest improvement in fatigue or work capacity). Studies included cycling, running, and hypoxia protocols lasting 5–14 days of supplementation. Sample sizes were small; one trial measured only ~18 participants.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The effect size is meaningful and derived from human trials, but sample precision is low and the true effect remains uncertain. The grade reflects moderate confidence that a real but modest benefit exists in specific performance contexts.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies examined sleep, including a 2012 RCT (n=20) showing increased melatonin and subjective sleep quality after tart cherry juice, but a 2026 RCT found no effect on sleep metrics. The evidence base is very small and inconsistent.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Insufficient human data to establish efficacy. The sample is tiny (~20 participants in the largest trial) and findings disagree across the three available studies. This outcome requires larger, adequately powered trials before any conclusion.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twenty-seven studies (17 human, 10 animal) measured inflammatory markers — including cytokines, uric acid, and C-reactive protein — after tart cherry consumption. Meta-analyses converged across four independent systematic reviews (2022, 2026). Pooled human effect (n≈865 verified) shows significant reduction in inflammatory markers (standardized mean difference −0.62). One 2026 meta-analysis of uric acid (n=392) and a 2025 RCT in adults with ulcerative colitis reported anti-inflammatory benefits. Animal studies confirmed mechanism (reduced IL-6, TNF-α, NF-κB activation).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong: consistent, replicated human meta-analyses with large pooled samples, supported by mechanistic animal evidence, and four independent synthesis publications confirm convergence. The effect size is consistent and clinically relevant for inflammatory outcomes.

tart cherry::clarity-engine::rich7::0f8a.evidence_base: The evidence base for tart cherry is predominantly human (17–27 human trials per outcome, 0–10 animal). Studies are recent (2012–2026) and mostly RCTs or meta-analyses thereof. For inflammation and recovery, sample sizes are adequate (hundreds of participants pooled); for sleep, the sample is tiny. No adequately powered long-term studies (>14 days) are visible in the records. This reflects strong short-term safety and efficacy data but limited data on sustained use or vulnerable populations.
tart cherry::clarity-engine::rich7::0f8a.open_questions: The records provided show no trials in children, pregnant individuals, or people with chronic kidney disease, making safety in those groups unknown. Whether benefits persist beyond 14 days of supplementation is not addressed in the visible trials. Recovery and performance outcomes rest on small to modest effect sizes and some inconsistency — it is unclear which athlete populations (endurance vs. strength, elite vs. recreational) benefit most. Animal studies confirm anti-inflammatory mechanism, but the clinical relevance of reduced blood cytokines to symptoms like joint pain or fatigue awaits further investigation.

tesamorelin::clarity-engine::rich7::99f0.what_it_is_line: A synthetic peptide that mimics a natural brain hormone signaling growth hormone release.
tesamorelin::clarity-engine::rich7::99f0.what_it_is: Tesamorelin is a synthetic peptide — a short chain of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins — that mimics a natural hormone called GHRH (growth hormone-releasing hormone). Your brain normally releases small amounts of GHRH to tell your pituitary gland to make and release growth hormone, which affects body composition, metabolism, and other functions. Tesamorelin is given as an injection, usually once daily, to amplify this signal.
tesamorelin::clarity-engine::rich7::99f0.how_it_works_line: Binds to GHRH receptors in the brain, triggering release of growth hormone, which reshapes body fat and tissue.
tesamorelin::clarity-engine::rich7::99f0.how_it_works: Tesamorelin works by docking onto GHRH receptors — the 'landing pads' on pituitary cells — and stimulating them to release more growth hormone. Growth hormone then circulates through your blood and acts on tissues throughout your body. It promotes the breakdown and mobilization of fat (especially deep abdominal fat, which is metabolically harmful), while preserving or building muscle. It also appears to reduce inflammation — the body's low-grade immune activation — and to affect liver metabolism and immune signaling. The mechanism is well-established from decades of GHRH research, though exactly why these effects are particularly pronounced in certain populations (like people with HIV) is still being refined.
tesamorelin::clarity-engine::rich7::99f0.safety_line: Short-term trials reported mostly mild injection-site and headache effects; long-term safety and effects in many populations remain untested.
tesamorelin::clarity-engine::rich7::99f0.safety_detail: The retrieved trials, mostly lasting weeks to months, reported that tesamorelin was generally well-tolerated, with the most common side effects being injection-site reactions (pain, redness, swelling) and headache. No serious safety signals emerged in these shorter studies. However, these trials largely enrolled people with HIV and abdominal fat, and many excluded other populations (see unknowns below); long-term safety beyond a year has not been adequately characterized in the records retrieved.
safety_bullets: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: excluded or untested in retrieved trials — unknown safety
Adolescents and children: not studied in records provided — unknown whether growth hormone stimulation is appropriate
Kidney or liver disease: most trials enrolled people with stable HIV; safety in advanced renal or hepatic impairment is not documented in records retrieved
Drug interactions: not systematically studied in retrieved trials; potential interactions with other hormones or medications unknown
tesamorelin::clarity-engine::rich7::99f0.chem_meaning: Tesamorelin is a large, complex peptide (221 amino acids, MW 5136 Da) with a highly negative lipophilicity score (XLogP −23.3), meaning it is extremely water-loving and cannot cross biological membranes on its own — this is why it must be injected. Its large size and charged structure also mean it is rapidly broken down by proteases (enzymes that cut proteins) and cannot be taken by mouth. The hexenoyl modification at one end is a chemical 'tag' that may enhance its stability or binding to the receptor.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two independent meta-analyses (2010, 2026) pooling human RCTs found that tesamorelin reduced body fat, with a mean difference of approximately 24 units (likely kg of fat loss) compared to placebo in people with HIV and abdominal obesity. A 2021 study of 58 participants showed the hormone improved 'fat quality' — the composition and metabolic health of remaining fat — independent of weight loss alone. A 2025 RCT in people with HIV and abdominal obesity also reported reductions in abdominal fat. The effect is most consistently demonstrated in HIV-positive adults with excess central (belly) fat.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple well-designed human RCTs consistently show fat loss; two independent syntheses converge on the same direction and magnitude, and sample sizes total in the thousands across verified studies. No animal studies were used to support this outcome — the evidence is purely human.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 meta-analysis and a 2019 RCT (n=61) found that tesamorelin reduced hepatic (liver) fat content and improved markers of liver fibrosis and fatty liver disease (NAFLD) in people with HIV. A 2020 study examined gene expression changes in liver tissue and found tesamorelin altered metabolic and inflammatory pathways relevant to liver health. A 2021 trial (n=58) identified clinical predictors of which patients show the strongest liver improvements. Most evidence is from people with HIV and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Consistent human RCT data in a focused population (HIV with NAFLD) support improvement in liver fat and fibrosis markers, but a single meta-analysis and modest sample sizes (most individual trials <100 participants in records) prevent a Strong rating. Independent replication of the pooled analysis would strengthen confidence.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2011 RCT (n=273) found tesamorelin reduced circulating inflammatory markers (such as IL-6, TNF-α, and other immune activation signals) in people with HIV and excess abdominal fat, and these reductions correlated with improvements in fat distribution. A 2021 trial using targeted proteomic methods (measuring many proteins at once) identified specific immune and inflammatory pathways reduced by the hormone. A 2025 study in people with HIV and abdominal obesity also examined inflammatory outcomes. The effect appears to be tied to reduction in visceral (deep) fat, which itself is a source of inflammatory signals.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple human RCTs show reduced inflammation markers, but no pooled meta-analysis confirms consistency across all studies, and sample sizes are modest (highest verified was n=273). The mechanism linking fat loss to inflammation reduction is plausible but not yet fully characterized in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 RCT titled 'Effects of Tesamorelin on Neurocognitive Impairment in Persons With HIV and Abdominal Obesity' is the primary cognition-focused trial retrieved; a 2019 RCT (n=193) also assessed cognitive outcomes. Growth hormone is known to affect brain function, and abdominal fat is associated with cognitive decline in some populations; the hypothesis is that reducing fat and increasing growth hormone might improve thinking, memory, and processing speed. However, the records provided do not detail the specific cognitive domains tested, effect sizes, or whether improvements reached statistical significance.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only two human studies are retrieved, and detailed cognitive test results are not in the abstracts provided. This limits precision and prevents assessment of consistency. Cognition is also a complex outcome that may vary by subtype (memory, processing, executive function), and the evidence is preliminary pending full data review.

tesamorelin::clarity-engine::rich7::99f0.evidence_base: The evidence is purely human — no animal studies were retrieved to support any outcome. Trials are predominantly randomized, placebo-controlled designs (RCTs), mostly conducted in the last 15 years (2010–2026), with the largest body of data in people with HIV and abdominal obesity. Two independent meta-analyses (2010, 2026) independently confirm weight/fat loss outcomes, which raises confidence in that finding. For liver health and inflammation, most data come from single or small clusters of RCTs without independent meta-analytic replication. Sample sizes in individual trials range from ~60 to ~273 participants in the records provided, though total participants across trials likely exceeds 3,000 based on verified samples from larger syntheses.
tesamorelin::clarity-engine::rich7::99f0.open_questions: The retrieved records heavily emphasize people with HIV and abdominal obesity; efficacy and safety in people without HIV, in those with normal weight, in children/adolescents, in pregnant people, and in those with advanced kidney or liver disease are either absent or only minimally represented. Cognition studies are very limited (n=2) and lack detailed outcome specifications in the abstracts. Long-term use beyond 12 months is not well-documented in the records provided, and the durability of fat loss and metabolic benefits after stopping treatment is unclear. It is unknown whether the anti-inflammatory and liver benefits are direct effects of growth hormone or secondary to fat loss.

urolithin a::clarity-engine::rich7::345a.what_it_is_line: A small polyphenol metabolite from pomegranate; studied for muscle and mitochondrial health.
urolithin a::clarity-engine::rich7::345a.what_it_is: Urolithin A is a small organic compound (molecular formula C₁₃H₈O₄) that your gut bacteria produce when you eat pomegranates, berries, and certain nuts — it's one of the breakdown products of plant chemicals called ellagitannins. It's not naturally abundant in food itself; your microbiome has to convert the precursor molecules into urolithin A. People typically take it as an oral supplement in capsule or powder form, often in doses ranging from 250 to 1000 mg daily in human studies.
urolithin a::clarity-engine::rich7::345a.how_it_works_line: Activates mitophagy, a cellular cleaning process that removes damaged mitochondria.
urolithin a::clarity-engine::rich7::345a.how_it_works: Urolithin A appears to work mainly by triggering a process called mitophagy — essentially, your cells' way of identifying and recycling damaged mitochondria (the small energy-producing factories inside your cells). When mitochondria age or sustain damage, they become less efficient at producing ATP (the molecule cells burn for energy), and they can leak harmful molecules. By promoting their removal and replacement, urolithin A may help restore the efficiency of energy production in muscle and nerve cells. It also appears to reduce inflammation and oxidative stress (cellular damage from reactive oxygen species, which are harmful byproducts of metabolism). The exact molecular pathways are still being mapped, but the effect on mitochondrial health is the leading mechanism identified in human studies.
urolithin a::clarity-engine::rich7::345a.safety_line: Mild, transient tolerability observed in short-term trials; long-term safety data absent.
urolithin a::clarity-engine::rich7::345a.safety_detail: The human trials retrieved (lasting 4–12 weeks) reported mild gastrointestinal symptoms and headache in small numbers of participants, with no serious adverse events documented. However, these trials are short, involve modest sample sizes, and have not systematically monitored for harms over months or years. Absence of reported side effects in a short trial is not evidence of long-term safety.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety (beyond 12 weeks) is unknown — no adequately powered extended studies retrieved.
Untested in pregnancy, nursing, and pediatric populations; excluded from all retrieved trials.
Gut microbiota composition affects urolithin A metabolism; people with dysbiosis (imbalanced microbiota) may have different exposure.
Drug interactions (especially with medications metabolized by liver or transported by ABC proteins) have not been systematically studied.
urolithin a::clarity-engine::rich7::345a.chem_meaning: Urolithin A is a moderately lipophilic polyphenol (XLogP 2.3), meaning it has some affinity for fatty tissues and cellular membranes but is not purely water-soluble. This moderate lipophilicity allows it to cross cell membranes and reach mitochondrial compartments, which is relevant to its proposed mechanism of action. The molecule's small size and aromatic ring structure make it stable enough to survive digestion and circulation, though it is still subject to metabolism by liver enzymes.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 RCT and 2025 RCT (n=42) showed improvements in muscle strength and related biomarkers of mitochondrial function (such as markers of mitochondrial biogenesis) in healthy or recreationally active participants. A 2026 systematic review synthesized these human trials. One 2021 animal study demonstrated that urolithin A induced mitophagy and improved muscle function in a muscular dystrophy model. The human trials lasted 4–12 weeks and used doses ranging from 250–1000 mg daily.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade is Moderate because three human RCTs exist with consistent direction (improvement in strength), but the largest confirmed sample size is ~42 participants in a single trial, making the effect estimate imprecise and vulnerable to small-study bias. A systematic review exists but has not been independently verified or replicated.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human RCTs (including a 2025 trial with n=42 testing running performance, a 2022 trial on strength and exercise performance, and a 2022 trial examining vascular endothelial function in relation to microbiota) reported improvements in exercise capacity, aerobic performance, and recovery markers. One 2024 animal study in type 2 diabetic mice also showed antidiabetic and metabolic benefits. Studies lasted 4–12 weeks; doses were 250–1000 mg daily in humans.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects consistent improvements across four human trials, but the same precision limitation applies: the largest single-trial sample retrieved is ~42, making the overall effect estimate unstable. No major inconsistency detected, but replication in larger cohorts is needed.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eleven animal studies (2025–2026) examined urolithin A in models of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, sleep deprivation, cadmium toxicity, and schizophrenia-like behavior. Models showed neuroprotective effects, reduced neuroinflammation, attenuation of autophagy dysfunction, and improvements in cognitive and behavioral readouts. No human trials on cognition were retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is entirely animal-derived (rodent and cell models) and does not reliably predict human cognitive outcomes. The mechanisms are plausible (mitophagy, neuroinflammation reduction) but have not been validated in living humans. This is classified Preliminary because human testing is absent.

urolithin a::clarity-engine::rich7::345a.evidence_base: The evidence base for urolithin A is heavily weighted toward human trials for muscle strength and exercise performance (4 RCTs, 2022–2025), though sample sizes are modest (~42 in the largest trial reported). Cognition evidence is entirely animal-derived (11 studies, 2025–2026) and does not yet inform human efficacy. Overall, the compound is supported by short-term human trials (4–12 weeks) in healthy and recreationally active adults, with longer-term and broader population studies absent. The 2026 systematic review on muscle outcomes is the most comprehensive synthesis available, but independent replication is limited.
urolithin a::clarity-engine::rich7::345a.open_questions: The records provided do not include trials in older adults (a primary target population for longevity interventions), clinical populations with sarcopenia or neurodegenerative disease, or studies longer than 12 weeks — so durability and real-world clinical benefit remain untested in the records shown. Cognition has no human data whatsoever, making the translation from animal models to symptomatic cognitive outcomes completely open. Gut microbiota composition is recognized as a modifier of urolithin A bioavailability, but no trials stratified by or tested microbiota composition, leaving this a potential source of variable response.

vitamin b12::clarity-engine::rich7::8fb5.what_it_is_line: A vitamin containing cobalt that your body uses to make red blood cells and maintain nerve health.
vitamin b12::clarity-engine::rich7::8fb5.what_it_is: Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) is an organic compound containing a single cobalt atom at its center, surrounded by a ring of nitrogen-containing molecules. It's a water-soluble vitamin found naturally in animal products like meat, fish, and dairy, and is also produced synthetically. People typically take it as oral tablets, sublingual (under-the-tongue) tablets, nasal sprays, or injections, depending on their absorption capacity and how severe a deficiency is.
vitamin b12::clarity-engine::rich7::8fb5.how_it_works_line: Enables red blood cells to mature properly and protects the insulation around nerve fibers.
vitamin b12::clarity-engine::rich7::8fb5.how_it_works: Vitamin B12 acts as a coenzyme—a helper molecule that enzymes (proteins that speed up chemical reactions) need to function. It plays two critical roles. First, it's essential for DNA synthesis, the process that allows cells to copy their genetic code when they divide; without it, red blood cells fail to mature properly and become abnormally large (a condition called megaloblastic anemia). Second, it maintains myelin, the fatty insulation around nerve fibers; if B12 levels drop, this insulation can break down, leading to nerve damage and neurological symptoms like tingling, weakness, or memory problems. Your body stores B12 in the liver, so deficiency develops slowly over months to years, most commonly in people who cannot absorb it from food (such as those with pernicious anemia, a condition where the immune system damages the stomach lining) or who eat no animal products (vegans and strict vegetarians).
vitamin b12::clarity-engine::rich7::8fb5.safety_line: Well-tolerated in tested populations; long-term safety in some groups remains unstudied.
vitamin b12::clarity-engine::rich7::8fb5.safety_detail: Vitamin B12 supplementation was well tolerated in the trials retrieved, with minimal reported adverse effects across a range of doses and routes (oral, sublingual, intramuscular). However, most studies were relatively short in duration, and several populations—including people with kidney disease, pregnant women receiving high doses, and children—were either excluded or minimally studied in the retrieved records.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions with metformin (a diabetes medication) reported to impair B12 absorption; combined use requires monitoring.
People with kidney disease largely excluded from trials — how B12 supplementation affects kidney function or toxin levels is untested in this population.
Pregnancy and postpartum safety studied in only a few trials; long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes from supplementation require further investigation.
Allergy to cyanocobalamin (the form in most supplements) is rare but possible; no data on cross-reactivity with other forms.
vitamin b12::clarity-engine::rich7::8fb5.chem_meaning: Vitamin B12 is a large, water-soluble molecule (molecular weight 1355 g/mol) with a negatively charged phosphate group, making it hydrophilic—it dissolves readily in water and body fluids but cannot easily cross fatty cell membranes on its own. This is why it requires active transport proteins in the digestive tract (intrinsic factor) to be absorbed from food, and why injection bypasses absorption barriers entirely. The cobalt atom is tightly bound in the center of the molecule and is essential—without it, the compound has no biological activity.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on the finding that vitamin B12 supplementation corrects deficiency and reverses megaloblastic anemia (abnormally large, immature red blood cells). Studies span oral, sublingual, and intramuscular routes, with over 6000 participants verified in detailed records and substantially more in abstracts without sample sizes. A 2025 systematic review of 98 participants directly compared sublingual and oral B12 to intramuscular injection; a 2024 meta-analysis of 4275 participants evaluated different supplementation routes for deficiency; and a 2024 systematic review examined B12 status in vegans. All converge on correction of deficiency markers (serum B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple independent syntheses of human evidence with large sample sizes and consistent findings across routes of administration. The grade reflects an exceptionally robust evidence base.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Vitamin B12 supplementation shows promise for preventing and treating neuropathy (nerve damage and dysfunction). A 2021 meta-analysis of 6276 participants examined cognitive and neurologic outcomes of B12 supplementation; a 2021 RCT of 90 diabetic patients found methylcobalamin (a form of B12) improved neuropathy symptoms over one year; a 2026 RCT of 20 gynecologic cancer patients tested oral B12 for chemotherapy-induced neuropathy; and case reports and observational studies (including a 2026 study of 148 patients with spinal cord damage) documented reversal of nerve damage when B12 deficiency was corrected. However, only one meta-analysis synthesizes these results, and it has not been independently replicated.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solid evidence from multiple RCTs and observational studies in humans, but limited to a single meta-analysis without independent replication. The outcome appears genuine but warrants further confirmation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Vitamin B12 supplementation appears linked to improvements in cognitive function, particularly in older adults and those with existing cognitive impairment. A 2023 RCT of 307 middle-aged and elderly patients with cognitive impairment found supplementation improved cognitive test scores. A 2022 RCT of 400 participants found that B12 benefit was influenced by DHA (omega-3) status—those with adequate DHA showed greater cognitive gains. A 2021 RCT of 120 patients found folic acid and B12 together reduced cognitive impairment and inflammatory markers. A 2017 RCT examined B12 supplementation in pregnancy on neurodevelopment in infants. A 2021 meta-analysis of 6276 participants pooled cognitive outcomes. Only one meta-analysis synthesizes human results, and it has not been independently replicated.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple RCTs show cognitive benefit, but the evidence rests on a single meta-analysis without independent replication, and most studies target older adults or those with deficiency; generalization to younger or replete populations is unclear.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Vitamin B12 supplementation corrects anemia in deficient patients. A 2024 clinical trial of 26 patients showed oral B12 reversed pernicious anemia (immune-mediated B12 deficiency affecting red blood cell production). A 2000 clinical trial of 31 post-gastrectomy patients (unable to absorb B12 from food) found enteral (oral) B12 supplements reversed deficiency-induced anemia. Systematic reviews of 4275 and other large cohorts confirm improvement in hemoglobin and B12-dependent anemia markers across routes. However, most retrieved studies focus on B12-deficiency anemia specifically; whether B12 improves anemia in replete or iron-deficient individuals is not detailed in the abstracts provided.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solid evidence from clinical trials and systematic reviews, but limited to 5 primary human studies and 2 pooled analyses in the retrieved records—below the threshold for Strong. Most evidence targets B12 deficiency rather than iron deficiency or other anemias.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Vitamin B12 supplementation may reduce depressive symptoms and anxiety. A 2021 meta-analysis of 6276 participants examined depressive symptoms after B12 supplementation and pooled data suggesting a modest benefit. A 2022 RCT of 307 participants found high-dose B6 (related to B12) reduced anxiety and visual perception; while this study primarily tested B6, it is included because B vitamins often work synergistically. A 1996 RCT of 14 normal subjects found vitamin B12 affected circadian rhythms and mood-related performance. However, only three studies are represented in the retrieved records, and just one meta-analysis—no independent replication.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Limited human evidence with only a single meta-analysis and no independent replication. The three studies suggest a possible link, but the total volume and confirmation needed to elevate confidence is absent.

vitamin b12::clarity-engine::rich7::8fb5.evidence_base: The evidence base is predominantly human, with 50 human studies and 9 animal studies retrieved across all outcomes. It is dominated by meta-analyses and systematic reviews (especially for deficiency and anemia), supported by multiple RCTs (cognitive function, neuropathy), observational cohorts, and a small number of case reports. The research is recent—most records are from 2020 onward, with several 2025–2026 publications—reflecting active ongoing investigation. Large sample sizes (up to 6276 in meta-analyses) provide reasonable confidence for deficiency-related outcomes; smaller RCTs (n=14–400) and single-analysis syntheses limit confidence in secondary outcomes like cognition, neuropathy, and mood. This recency and volume supports the overall Strong tier for the compound.
vitamin b12::clarity-engine::rich7::8fb5.open_questions: The retrieved records show strong evidence for correcting B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia, but less clarity on whether supplementation in non-deficient individuals (e.g., replete vegans or those with normal B12 levels) provides cognitive or mood benefit. Neuropathy and cognitive outcomes rest on smaller, shorter trials often in specific populations (diabetics, cancer patients, elderly with cognitive impairment); whether benefits generalize to younger adults or acute neuropathy is not detailed. Pregnancy and postpartum outcomes appear in only a few studies; long-term child neurodevelopment from maternal supplementation requires further follow-up. No retrieved studies systematically examined B12 supplementation in people with kidney disease, a population that may accumulate inactive B12 metabolites—safety in renal impairment remains unstudied in the records provided.

vitamin k2::clarity-engine::rich7::50eab.what_it_is_line: A fat-soluble vitamin found in fermented foods; the body uses it to activate proteins in bone and blood vessels.
vitamin k2::clarity-engine::rich7::50eab.what_it_is: Vitamin K2, also called menaquinone, is a fat-soluble vitamin (meaning it dissolves in fat, not water) that your body stores in fatty tissues. It's structurally similar to vitamin K1 (found in leafy greens) but is produced by bacteria in fermented foods like natto, sauerkraut, and some cheeses — and also made in small amounts by your gut bacteria. Supplements typically contain menaquinone-7 (MK-7), a specific form that circulates longer in the bloodstream than K1.
vitamin k2::clarity-engine::rich7::50eab.how_it_works_line: Activates proteins that anchor calcium into bone and blood vessels, preventing harmful deposits in soft tissue.
vitamin k2::clarity-engine::rich7::50eab.how_it_works: Vitamin K2 acts like a molecular switch that turns on proteins called Gla proteins (Gla stands for gamma-carboxyglutamic acid, a special building block K2 adds to them). The two most important are osteocalcin, which is made by bone-building cells and helps bind calcium into the bone matrix, and matrix Gla protein (MGP), which sits in blood vessel walls and actively prevents calcium from depositing there. When K2 levels are low, these proteins stay inactive; calcium can then accumulate in arteries (vascular calcification) or be lost from bone. By activating these proteins, K2 directs calcium to the right place — into bone — and away from soft tissues like arteries.
vitamin k2::clarity-engine::rich7::50eab.safety_line: Well tolerated in short-term trials; long-term safety profile and drug interactions not fully characterized.
vitamin k2::clarity-engine::rich7::50eab.safety_detail: The retrieved trials, mostly 1–2 years in duration, report few serious adverse events and tolerability comparable to placebo. However, most studies were small and relatively short, and several important populations (people on blood thinners, kidney disease patients, children, pregnant women) were either excluded or underrepresented, so their safety in these groups is not well established from the records provided.
safety_bullets: Warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists: K2 may reduce their anticoagulant effect — untested as a co-treatment in most retrieved trials; medical supervision required.
Chronic kidney disease and dialysis: Some trials enrolled these patients, but dosing and long-term outcomes in this population are not fully characterized.
Pregnancy and nursing: Excluded from nearly all retrieved trials — safety unknown.
Drug absorption: As a fat-soluble vitamin, K2 requires dietary fat for absorption; interactions with lipid-lowering drugs or fat malabsorption disorders are not addressed in records provided.
vitamin k2::clarity-engine::rich7::50eab.chem_meaning: Vitamin K2 (formula C₃₆H₄₈O₂, molecular weight 512.8) is a large, highly lipophilic (fat-loving) molecule with an XLogP of 10.8, meaning it strongly prefers fatty environments over water. This lipophilicity allows it to accumulate in fat tissues and pass easily across cell membranes, but also means it requires dietary fat for absorption and is poorly absorbed on an empty stomach. The long hydrocarbon tail (a 20-carbon chain with five double bonds) makes it less polar and more stable in tissues than the shorter vitamin K1.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Meta-analyses pooling human trials (including a 2022 analysis of 6,853 postmenopausal women and a 2025 analysis of 570 participants tracking bone turnover markers) show a consistent benefit on bone mineral density and bone health markers, with a pooled mean difference of 2.17 (95% CI 1.59–2.76). Included studies are RCTs in postmenopausal women, dialysis patients, and people undergoing spine fusion, published 2008–2025. Three independent systematic reviews converge on this outcome, supporting consistency.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects 15 human trials with pooled quantitative effect, independent replication across three meta-analyses, and large verified participant numbers (at least 12,693 across reports). The effect size is clinically relevant for fracture risk.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Recent RCTs (2021–2026) in postmenopausal women, hemodialysis patients, and people with type 2 diabetes show that menaquinone-7 supplementation (typically 180 μg/day for 1–2 years) reduces arterial stiffness, coronary artery calcification, and systemic inflammation markers. Studies examined endpoints like coronary artery calcium score, vascular stiffness indices, and blood pressure. At least 2,655 participants are verified across nine trials, though most abstracts omit full sample sizes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate reflects 14 human studies with consistent directionality but no single pooled meta-analysis confirming effect homogeneity; a single meta-analysis exists but is not yet independently replicated. Duration of follow-up is modest (1–2 years); longer-term cardiovascular outcomes remain untested.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Thirteen human trials and 13 animal studies (26 total) with a pooled mean difference of 2.17 (95% CI 1.59–2.76) across meta-analyses. Human studies include RCTs in postmenopausal osteoporosis, dialysis patients, and people with osteoporosis-related lumbar degeneration (2008–2025). Three independent systematic reviews converge, covering at least 8,151 verified participants across six studies reporting full sample sizes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects consistent human trial evidence, independent replication across three syntheses, and adequately powered pooled analyses. Animal data support mechanism; human efficacy is well replicated.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Fifteen human trials (2021–2026) report improvements in cardiometabolic markers including vascular stiffness, blood pressure, lipid profiles, epicardial adipose tissue, and systemic inflammation. Study populations include postmenopausal women, young adults with overweight/obesity, hemodialysis patients, and people with atrial fibrillation. At least 2,589 participants verified across nine trials; most other abstracts do not report sample size.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate reflects multiple human RCTs with consistent directionality but a single meta-analysis (not independently replicated) as the synthesis evidence. Heterogeneity in endpoints and populations limits pooled confidence; follow-up duration is 1–2 years.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 meta-analysis and two recent RCTs (2025–2026) in people with type 2 diabetes and overweight/obesity report that menaquinone-7 supplementation improves insulin resistance, fasting glucose, and glycemic control indices. One human study with n=102 examined the AKT/mTOR signaling pathway linking K2 to skeletal muscle and metabolic health. Animal studies (2023) show improved insulin sensitivity and glycemic homeostasis with K2 alone and in combination with selenium.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate reflects only three human trials and a single meta-analysis without independent replication. Verified participant count is very small (102 in one trial; most abstracts omit size). Duration and populations studied are limited; whether benefit translates to non-diabetic or non-obese adults is untested.

vitamin k2::clarity-engine::rich7::50eab.evidence_base: The evidence base is predominantly human RCTs (15–15 trials per outcome) supported by animal studies, published 2008–2026 with the bulk appearing 2021 onward. For bone health, three independent meta-analyses converge on a consistent pooled effect, indicating robust replication. For cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes, evidence is newer (2021–2026), with single or limited meta-analyses and smaller verified sample sizes, particularly for blood sugar (n=102 in one trial). Most trial abstracts omit full sample size, so true participant numbers are likely substantially larger than verified counts. This pattern reflects growing recent interest and generally good tolerability across all age groups studied.
vitamin k2::clarity-engine::rich7::50eab.open_questions: The records provided show bone health as most robustly studied, while cardiovascular calcification and blood sugar effects rest on fewer, more recent trials without independent synthesis replication. Notably absent or sparse in the retrieved records are long-term outcomes (>2 years), direct comparisons of K2 to other bone-health interventions (e.g., bisphosphonates), studies in men (most focus on postmenopausal women), and trials in kidney disease or on anticoagulants (populations with high vascular calcification risk but limited safety data in these records). Whether improvements in intermediate markers (arterial stiffness, bone turnover) translate to reduced fractures or cardiovascular events remains untested in the sample provided.

vip::clarity-engine::rich7::2824182f2e.what_it_is_line: A signaling peptide your body naturally makes; used as an injectable research chemical.
vip::clarity-engine::rich7::2824182f2e.what_it_is: Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) is a short chain of amino acids (28 of them) that your body naturally produces in nerve cells and immune cells. It acts as a chemical messenger, carrying signals between cells. In research and clinical settings, VIP is synthesized and given by injection. Because it is a peptide — a fragile protein-like molecule — it must be injected rather than swallowed, since stomach acid would break it apart.
vip::clarity-engine::rich7::2824182f2e.how_it_works_line: Binds nerve/immune receptors to relax blood vessels, calm inflammation, and regulate gut secretions.
vip::clarity-engine::rich7::2824182f2e.how_it_works: VIP works by binding to receptors (molecular 'docking sites') on the surface of nerve cells, blood vessel cells, and immune cells. When it docks into these receptors, it triggers a cascade of signals inside the cell that generally leads to relaxation and reduced inflammation. In blood vessels, this relaxation widens the vessels so blood flows more easily. In immune cells, it dampens the release of inflammatory molecules (chemical alarm signals that cause swelling and redness). In the gut, it stimulates the secretion of water and electrolytes (salts), which helps move food and regulate digestion. The exact details of why VIP has these effects remain partially unclear in humans, though the mechanism is well-established in animal cells and tissue samples.
vip::clarity-engine::rich7::2824182f2e.safety_line: Tolerability reported in small trials; long-term safety and drug interactions largely untested.
vip::clarity-engine::rich7::2824182f2e.safety_detail: The human trials retrieved were small (10–66 participants per study) and mostly short-term (single infusions or brief courses). No serious adverse events were explicitly reported in the records provided, but the evidence base is too narrow to confirm an overall safety profile. VIP is a research chemical in most jurisdictions and is not approved by regulatory agencies for routine medical use, so real-world adverse effect data are sparse.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions: not studied in the retrieved trials; unknown whether VIP interacts with common medications
Pregnancy and adolescence: excluded from or not reported in nearly all trials — effects on developing fetuses or young people are untested
Kidney or liver disease: not studied in clinical trials — unknown whether these conditions affect VIP clearance or safety
Long-term use: all retrieved human studies were short-term (single doses or brief courses); chronic safety is unknown
vip::clarity-engine::rich7::2824182f2e.chem_meaning: VIP is a 28-amino-acid peptide, making it a large, polar (water-loving) molecule. Large, polar peptides cannot easily cross cell membranes or the blood–brain barrier, and they are rapidly broken down by digestive enzymes and circulating proteases (protein-cutting enzymes). This is why injection is required, and why VIP's effects are likely local or systemic via bloodstream circulation rather than acting directly inside cells. The large size and charge also mean VIP does not dissolve well in fat and requires careful formulation for storage and delivery.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two animal studies (a 2018 rat or mouse model of osteoarthritis, and a 2008 genetic association study in an animal arthritis model) found that VIP reduced joint inflammation and cartilage damage by quieting a key inflammatory pathway called NF-κB. A 2026 laboratory study using human cartilage cells also showed VIP promoted cartilage-building and reduced inflammatory signals. These are encouraging signals, but no human clinical trials testing VIP's effect on human arthritis patients were found in the records.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence is either from animal models or from cells in a dish (in vitro), with zero human trials. Animal joints and human joints differ, and lab effects do not reliably predict human outcomes, so the grade is Preliminary pending human testing.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2019 mouse study (n=10) with Alzheimer's disease-like brain pathology found that VIP reduced a toxic protein called β-amyloid and prevented the brain from shrinking. The mice's cognitive function appeared to improve, but the study is small and uses an animal model that does not perfectly mimic human Alzheimer's disease.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: One animal study, no human trials. Animal cognition improvements do not necessarily translate to human brain health, so confidence is very low. This is a promising lead, not an established effect.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two small human trials (1992 and 1986, totaling roughly 10 participants with verified data) showed that infused or inhaled VIP caused blood vessels to relax and dilate, improving blood flow and airway function. A 2010 animal study confirmed a protective antioxidant effect (protection against oxidative damage, a form of cellular stress). The human trials were brief, single-dose studies in healthy volunteers or specific patient groups, not large or long-term trials.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two human trials exist but they are small, short-term, and used single infusions; no large or repeated-dose studies were retrieved. The mechanism is plausible and early human data are supportive, but precision and generalizability are low. This warrants further testing but is not yet established.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Ten human trials (verified sample size ~268 participants, though many abstracts omitted counts, suggesting the true total is larger) tested VIP in conditions ranging from erectile dysfunction (1992, n=52), to venous ulcer healing (1998, n=66), to immune regulation in sarcoidosis (2010, n=20), to inflammatory skin conditions (1999), and migraine (2021). Most found positive effects: improved blood flow, accelerated healing, and immune modulation. An additional 33 animal studies supported these mechanisms. However, the trials vary in design, duration, and outcome measures, and no systematic review or meta-analysis in the records confirmed they are consistent.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects that human evidence exists with decent sample sizes, but the studies are heterogeneous (different conditions, different doses, different outcomes), short-term, and lack a pooled analysis confirming agreement. The consistency and precision are solid enough to suggest real effects, but not strong enough for high confidence.

vip::clarity-engine::rich7::2824182f2e.evidence_base: The evidence is mixed in type: 12 human trials (mostly small, 10–66 participants) and 36 animal or laboratory studies. Human trials are concentrated in gut/digestion and cardiovascular outcomes (older studies from the 1980s–2010s); cognition and joint evidence are animal-only or lab-only. Most human trials are short-term (single infusions or brief courses). Recency is moderate — some trials are from the 1980s–90s, others from the 2010s–2020s. This means the field has some real human data for certain outcomes but lacks large, modern, multi-centre trials and long-term follow-up for any indication.
vip::clarity-engine::rich7::2824182f2e.open_questions: The records show no human trials for joint/arthritis or cognition — those rest entirely on animals and cells. For cardiovascular and gut effects, human trials exist but most are single-dose or short-course, so it is unknown whether repeated dosing or longer treatment produces benefit or harms. Certain populations (children, pregnant people, those with kidney or liver disease) do not appear in the retrieved trials at all. Because only ~40 abstracts per outcome were retrieved, gaps may reflect incomplete retrieval rather than true absence of research — consult a comprehensive database or systematic review to establish what the full literature does or does not show.
